sections.title: The pen and the Moon: one force, not two

board_events.text: One law for the falling pen and the orbiting Moon
For centuries, heaven and earth were thought to follow different rules.

board_events.caption: Throw it fast enough and the ground curves away as fast as it falls

board_events.text: Harder throw lands farther; fast enough, and it never lands at all.
An orbit is perpetual falling — missing the Earth forever.
The Moon: a stone thrown sideways fast enough to keep missing.
The pen's pull and the Moon's pull are the same force.
Newton, at twenty-three, first saw the two as one.

segments.text: <curious>Here is the boldest idea in all of physics: the falling pen in your hand and the Moon circling overhead obey one and the same law, not two.
For thousands of years people split the universe in two: the heavens ran on one set of rules, earthly objects on another. Newton erased that line.
Picture standing on a tall hill and throwing a cricket ball flat out. It curves down and lands. Throw harder, it lands farther away.
Now throw it impossibly hard. The ball keeps falling toward the centre, but the round Earth curves away beneath it at exactly the same rate.
So it never gets closer to the ground. It just falls around the Earth forever. That is an orbit.
The Moon is doing nothing fancier than this: a stone thrown sideways so fast that it keeps missing the Earth.
<excited>And the punchline: the exact force that pulls your pen to the floor is the force keeping the Moon in the sky.
A twenty-three year old Isaac Newton was the first to see clearly that these were one thing.
<curious>Physics का सबसे bold idea यही है: आपका गिरता हुआ pen और सिर के ऊपर घूमता Moon, दोनों एक ही law को follow करते हैं, अलग-अलग नहीं।
हज़ारों सालों तक लोग universe को दो हिस्सों में बाँटते थे: heavens का अलग rule, earthly objects का अलग। Newton ने वो line मिटा दी।
एक ऊँची hill पर खड़े होकर एक cricket ball को सीधा फेंकने की कल्पना कीजिए। वो नीचे curve होकर गिरती है। ज़ोर से फेंकें, तो और दूर गिरती है।
अब इसे बहुत ज़्यादा ज़ोर से फेंकिए। ball लगातार centre की तरफ गिरती रहती है, पर गोल Earth उसके नीचे से उतनी ही तेज़ी से मुड़ जाती है।
तो वो कभी ज़मीन के पास नहीं आती। बस हमेशा के लिए Earth के चारों ओर गिरती रहती है। यही एक orbit है।
Moon इससे ज़्यादा कुछ special नहीं कर रहा: एक पत्थर जो इतनी तेज़ side में फेंका गया कि वो Earth को miss करता रहता है।
<excited>और असली punchline: जो force आपके pen को floor पर खींचता है, वही force Moon को आसमान में टिकाए रखता है।
तेईस साल के Isaac Newton पहले इंसान थे जिन्होंने साफ़ देखा कि ये दोनों एक ही चीज़ हैं।

board_events.text: Every mass tugs on every other mass

board_events.text: Pulled toward book, neighbour, Sun, a far galaxy — all together.
Two protons: electric push is about $10^{36}$ times their gravitational pull.
Gravity only wins when mass piles up hugely — like a whole planet.
Earth's pull rules your day: walking, dropping a spoon.
Your own pull on that spoon is far too tiny to notice.
Weak — but never zero, and never shielded away.

segments.text: Newton's law says something almost eerie: every chunk of matter in the universe is quietly tugging on every other chunk.
Right this second you are being pulled toward your physics book, toward the person beside you, toward the Sun, even toward a distant galaxy.
So why has no textbook ever slid across your desk to greet you? Because gravity is staggeringly weak.
Take two protons. The electric force shoving them apart is about ten to the thirty-six times stronger than the gravity pulling them together.
Gravity only becomes a big player when you pile up a colossal amount of mass, like an entire planet.
That is exactly why the Earth's pull dominates everything you do, from walking to dropping a spoon.
Yet your own pull on that spoon, or on your book, is far too tiny to ever notice.
<curious>Weak, yes — but gravity is never zero and, as we will see, can never be switched off.
Newton का law कुछ अजीब-सा कहता है: universe में matter का हर टुकड़ा, बाकी हर टुकड़े को चुपचाप खींच रहा है।
इसी पल आप अपनी physics book की तरफ, बगल वाले इंसान की तरफ, Sun की तरफ, यहाँ तक कि एक दूर galaxy की तरफ भी खिंच रहे हैं।
तो कोई textbook कभी आपके desk पर खिसककर आपसे मिलने क्यों नहीं आई? क्योंकि gravity बेहद weak है।
दो protons लीजिए। उन्हें अलग धकेलने वाला electric force, उन्हें जोड़ने वाली gravity से लगभग दस की power thirty-six गुना ज़्यादा strong है।
Gravity तभी एक बड़ा player बनती है जब बहुत भारी मात्रा में mass इकट्ठा हो — जैसे एक पूरा planet।
इसीलिए Earth का pull आपके हर काम पर हावी रहता है, चलने से लेकर चम्मच गिराने तक।
फिर भी उस चम्मच पर, या आपकी book पर आपका खुद का pull इतना छोटा है कि कभी महसूस ही नहीं होता।
<curious>Weak, हाँ — पर gravity कभी zero नहीं होती, और जैसा आगे देखेंगे, इसे कभी बंद नहीं किया जा सकता।

sections.title: When you may use the clean formula: points and spheres

board_events.text: The clean formula is written for point masses
$F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ assumes size is tiny beside separation.

board_events.caption: A uniform sphere acts as a point mass at its centre

board_events.text: Safe case 1: two genuine point particles.
Safe case 2: two uniform spheres; use centre-to-centre $r$.
Safe case 3: a uniform sphere and a point mass.
Rod, ring, arc, L-shape? Do NOT plug in — integrate.
Point formula on a rod = a classic mark-loser.

segments.text: The law you are about to meet is written, strictly, for point masses — objects so small beside their separation that their size does not matter.
In symbols, F equals big G times m one m two divided by r squared, and that single r assumes one clean, well-defined distance.
<curious>So can you use it on real, chunky bodies? Often yes — thanks to a gorgeous result Newton proved, called the shell theorem.
The first safe case is the simplest: two genuine point particles, the original setting of the law.
The second: two uniform spheres. The shell theorem lets each sphere act as a point at its centre, with r measured centre to centre.
The third is a mix: a uniform sphere together with a point mass. Those three, and only those three, are safe to plug straight in.
But a rod, a thin ring, an arc, an L-shaped body? Different pieces sit at different distances, so you must add up — integrate — every tiny pull.
Misapplying the point-mass formula to a rod is one of the most common ways students quietly lose marks.
जो law आप देखने वाले हैं, वो strictly point masses के लिए लिखा गया है — ऐसे objects जो अपनी separation के मुक़ाबले इतने छोटे हों कि उनका size मायने ही न रखे।
Symbols में, F बराबर big G into m one m two, divided by r squared; और वो अकेला r एक साफ़, well-defined distance मान लेता है।
<curious>तो क्या इसे असली, भारी-भरकम bodies पर use कर सकते हैं? अक्सर हाँ — Newton के साबित किए एक ख़ूबसूरत result की बदौलत, जिसे shell theorem कहते हैं।
पहला safe case सबसे आसान है: दो असली point particles, यानी law का original setting।
दूसरा: दो uniform spheres। shell theorem हर sphere को उसके centre पर एक point की तरह act करने देता है, और r को centre to centre नापा जाता है।
तीसरा एक mix है: एक uniform sphere के साथ एक point mass। बस यही तीन, और सिर्फ़ यही तीन, सीधे plug करने के लिए safe हैं।
पर एक rod, एक पतला ring, एक arc, या एक L-shaped body? अलग-अलग हिस्से अलग-अलग distances पर होते हैं, तो हर छोटे pull को जोड़ना — integrate करना — ज़रूरी है।
एक rod पर point-mass formula को ग़लत लगाना, students के चुपचाप marks गँवाने के सबसे common तरीक़ों में से एक है।

sections.title: Two masses that turn out equal: gravitational and inertial

board_events.text: Mass wears two different hats
In gravitation, $m$ is gravitational mass $m_g$ — how strongly a body joins in gravity.
In $F=m_i a$, $m$ is inertial mass $m_i$ — its resistance to acceleration.
Logically, no reason these two should be equal.

board_events.caption: Different masses, same $g$ — because $m_g=m_i$

board_events.text: Experiment: equal to better than one part in $10^{12}$.
In $m_g\,g=m_i a$ the masses cancel only if $m_g=m_i$.
Einstein's Equivalence Principle — the seed of General Relativity.

segments.text: Here is a subtle point examiners love. The very word mass secretly names two different properties.
In Newton's law of gravitation, the m is gravitational mass — a measure of how strongly a body takes part in gravity, both pulling and being pulled.
But mass also appears in F equals m a, where it is inertial mass — a measure of how stubbornly a body resists being accelerated.
Logically these are unrelated. There is no obvious reason a body's gravitational charge should equal its resistance to being pushed.
And yet — drop a light ball and a heavy ball together, and they fall at the same rate, hammer and feather alike on the airless Moon.
Experiment confirms the two masses are equal to better than one part in ten to the twelve. A staggering coincidence.
Watch why it matters: in the equation gravitational mass times g equals inertial mass times a, the two masses cancel only because they are equal, leaving the same g for every body.
<excited>Einstein elevated this coincidence into his Principle of Equivalence — that gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable — the seed of General Relativity.
यहाँ एक subtle point है जो examiners को बहुत पसंद है। mass शब्द असल में दो अलग properties को चुपके से नाम देता है।
Newton के law of gravitation में m यानी gravitational mass — यह measure करता है कि एक body gravity में कितनी strongly हिस्सा लेती है, खींचने और खिंचने दोनों में।
पर mass, F बराबर m a में भी आता है, जहाँ यह inertial mass है — यानी body accelerate होने का कितना ज़िद्दी होकर विरोध करती है।
Logically ये दोनों अलग हैं। कोई साफ़ वजह नहीं कि किसी body का gravitational charge, उसके push का विरोध करने के बराबर हो।
और फिर भी — एक हल्की और एक भारी ball साथ गिराइए, दोनों एक ही rate से गिरती हैं; airless Moon पर hammer और feather भी एक साथ।
Experiment confirm करता है कि दोनों masses दस की power twelve में एक हिस्से से भी बेहतर बराबर हैं। एक हैरान करने वाला coincidence।
देखिए क्यों मायने रखता है: gravitational mass into g बराबर inertial mass into a में, दोनों masses सिर्फ़ इसलिए cancel होते हैं क्योंकि वे बराबर हैं, और हर body के लिए वही g बचता है।
<excited>Einstein ने इस coincidence को अपने Principle of Equivalence तक उठाया — कि gravity और acceleration locally एक जैसे हैं — यही General Relativity का बीज बना।

sections.title: Why the exponent is exactly two: reading it off Kepler

board_events.text: Where does the inverse-square law come from?
Newton reasoned backward from Kepler's planetary data.

board_events.caption: A planet needs a centre-seeking force to stay on its circle

board_events.text: All but $m$ and $r$ is constant, so $F\propto m/r^2$.
Newton's 3rd law $\Rightarrow$ symmetric: $F=\dfrac{GM_s m}{r^2}$.
The Moon test confirmed the same law rules the heavens.

segments.text: Newton's law is fundamental — we do not derive it from something deeper. But there is a classic argument, the one the board asks for, showing why the exponent must be exactly two.
The trick is to reason backward from what Kepler had already observed about the planets, and demand that gravity reproduce it.
Take a planet on a circular orbit around the Sun. A body moving in a circle is always accelerating toward the centre, so some force must supply that inward pull.
That required centripetal force is m v squared over r. Newton's leap was to say: this inward force is gravity itself.
In one period T the planet covers the circumference two pi r, so its speed is two pi r over T. Substitute, and the force becomes four pi squared m r over T squared.
Now bring in Kepler's third law, T squared proportional to r cubed. Write T squared as k r cubed and substitute: the force becomes a constant times m over r squared.
Everything except the planet's mass m and the distance r is a fixed constant. So force is proportional to m over r squared — the inverse square appears on its own.
By Newton's third law the planet pulls the Sun just as hard, so the law must be symmetric in both masses: F equals big G M sub s m over r squared.
<excited>Newton then checked this against the Moon's orbit — the famous Moon test — and the agreement was spectacular.
Newton का law fundamental है — हम इसे किसी और गहरी चीज़ से derive नहीं करते। पर एक classic argument है, वही जो board पूछता है, जो दिखाता है कि exponent बिलकुल two ही क्यों होना चाहिए।
Trick यह है कि Kepler ने planets के बारे में जो पहले से observe किया था, उससे उल्टा reason करें, और demand करें कि gravity उसे reproduce करे।
एक planet को Sun के चारों ओर circular orbit पर लीजिए। circle में घूमता body हमेशा centre की तरफ accelerate होता है, तो कोई force उस inward pull को देना ही चाहिए।
वो ज़रूरी centripetal force है m v squared over r। Newton का बड़ा कदम यह था: यही inward force ख़ुद gravity है।
एक period T में planet circumference two pi r तय करता है, तो उसकी speed two pi r over T है। substitute कीजिए, और force बन जाता है four pi squared m r over T squared।
अब Kepler का third law लाइए, T squared proportional to r cubed। T squared को k r cubed लिखकर substitute कीजिए: force एक constant into m over r squared बन जाता है।
Planet के mass m और distance r को छोड़कर बाक़ी सब एक fixed constant है। तो force, m over r squared के proportional है — inverse square अपने-आप निकल आता है।
Newton के third law से planet, Sun को उतनी ही ज़ोर से खींचता है, तो law दोनों masses में symmetric होना चाहिए: F बराबर big G M s m over r squared।
<excited>फिर Newton ने इसे Moon की orbit पर check किया — मशहूर Moon test — और agreement शानदार था।

board_events.text: Minus sign = attraction: force points back toward the other mass.
Every particle attracts every other, along the line joining them.
Force $\propto m_1 m_2$ and $\propto 1/r^2$.
Attractive, central, along the line of centres — always.

segments.text: <curious>Now the law itself, in the form you will use on every single problem.
The magnitude is F equals big G times m one m two over r squared. Double either mass and the force doubles; double the distance and the force drops to a quarter.
The two bodies pull each other equally and oppositely, straight along the line joining their centres — Newton's third law in action.
In vector form, the force on m one due to m two is minus big G m one m two over r squared, times the unit vector pointing from m two to m one.
That minus sign carries the single most important fact: gravity is always attractive, so the force points back toward the other mass, never away.
In words: every particle in the universe attracts every other, directly as the product of their masses and inversely as the square of their separation, along the line joining them.
So force climbs with the product of the masses and falls as one over r squared.
Gravity is attractive, central, and always directed along the line of centres.
<curious>अब ख़ुद law, उसी form में जिसे आप हर problem पर use करेंगे।
Magnitude है F बराबर big G into m one m two over r squared। कोई भी mass double करो तो force double; distance double करो तो force एक-चौथाई रह जाता है।
दोनों bodies एक-दूसरे को बराबर और opposite खींचती हैं, ठीक centres को जोड़ने वाली line के साथ — Newton's third law काम पर।
Vector form में, m two की वजह से m one पर force है minus big G m one m two over r squared, into वो unit vector जो m two से m one की तरफ point करता है।
वो minus sign सबसे अहम fact रखता है: gravity हमेशा attractive है, तो force हमेशा दूसरे mass की तरफ वापस point करता है, कभी दूर नहीं।
शब्दों में: universe का हर particle हर दूसरे को खींचता है, उनके masses के product के directly proportional और उनकी separation के square के inversely proportional, joining line के साथ।
तो force masses के product के साथ बढ़ता है और one over r squared के हिसाब से घटता है।
Gravity attractive है, central है, और हमेशा centres की line के साथ directed है।

board_events.text: Independent of mass, medium, time, place, temperature.
A scalar, and the smallest of the fundamental constants.
Physically, $G$ = force between two $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ masses $1\,\mathrm{m}$ apart.
Dimensions from $G=Fr^2/(m_1 m_2)$.

segments.text: We keep writing big G. What is it, really?
Its measured value is six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven, in newton metre squared per kilogram squared. That tiny number is why gravity is so gentle.
Here is its physical meaning: big G is simply the gravitational force, in newtons, between two one-kilogram masses placed one metre apart.
Its dimensional formula is M to the minus one, L cubed, T to the minus two. Worth memorising — it turns up in dimensional-analysis questions.
Crucially, big G is a true universal constant. It does not change with the masses, the medium between them, the time, the place, or the temperature.
It is a scalar, and the smallest in magnitude of all the fundamental constants — the deep reason gravity feels so feeble.
Say it once more, because it anchors everything: G is the pull between two one-kilogram masses one metre apart — which is why it is so small.
<whisper>Exam trick: to recover its dimensions, just rearrange the law as G equals F r squared over m one m two.
हम बार-बार big G लिखते हैं। असल में यह है क्या?
इसकी measured value है six point six seven into ten to the minus eleven, newton metre squared per kilogram squared में। यही छोटा-सा number gravity को इतना gentle बनाता है।
इसका physical meaning: big G बस दो one-kilogram masses के बीच का gravitational force है, जब वे one metre दूर रखे हों।
इसका dimensional formula है M to the minus one, L cubed, T to the minus two। याद रखने लायक़ — यह dimensional-analysis questions में आता है।
अहम बात: big G एक true universal constant है। यह masses, बीच के medium, time, place, या temperature के साथ नहीं बदलता।
यह एक scalar है, और सभी fundamental constants में magnitude में सबसे छोटा — यही गहरी वजह है कि gravity इतनी feeble लगती है।
एक बार फिर कहते हैं, क्योंकि यही सब कुछ anchor करता है: G दो one-kilogram masses के बीच का pull है जब वे one metre दूर हों — इसीलिए यह इतना छोटा है।
<whisper>Exam trick: इसके dimensions निकालने के लिए law को rearrange कीजिए, G बराबर F r squared over m one m two।

board_events.text: Compute each pairwise force as if the others were absent.
Add head-to-tail as vectors — never as bare numbers.
Equal pulls at an angle do NOT simply double — resolve first.
Resolve into $x,y$; add component-wise; recombine.
$F_{\text{net}}=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}$, then the direction.

segments.text: Real problems rarely have just two masses. What is the net pull on one particle from many others?
The principle of superposition answers it: fix the target particle, and draw an arrow toward every other mass, since gravity attracts.
The net force is the vector sum of all the pairwise forces — big G m one m i over r one i squared, summed over every other mass i, each along its own direction.
The key subtlety: compute each pairwise force entirely on its own, as though the other masses were simply not there.
Then combine them head to tail, as vectors. Adding their magnitudes directly is only allowed when the forces happen to be collinear.
<curious>Two equal pulls meeting at an angle do not just double. Depending on the angle they may partly cancel — so never shortcut.
The safe recipe is always the same: resolve each force into x and y components, and add the components separately.
Then recombine with F net equals the root of F x squared plus F y squared, and read off the direction.
असली problems में शायद ही सिर्फ़ दो masses होते हैं। कई दूसरों की वजह से एक particle पर net pull क्या होगा?
Superposition का principle इसका जवाब देता है: target particle को fix कीजिए, और हर दूसरे mass की तरफ एक arrow खींचिए, क्योंकि gravity attract करती है।
Net force सभी pairwise forces का vector sum है — big G m one m i over r one i squared, हर दूसरे mass i पर sum किया गया, हर एक अपनी direction के साथ।
अहम subtlety: हर pairwise force को पूरी तरह अकेले compute कीजिए, जैसे बाक़ी masses वहाँ हों ही नहीं।
फिर उन्हें head to tail, vectors की तरह जोड़िए। उनके magnitudes को सीधे जोड़ना सिर्फ़ तभी allowed है जब forces collinear हों।
<curious>एक angle पर मिलती दो बराबर pulls सिर्फ़ double नहीं होतीं। angle के हिसाब से वे आंशिक रूप से cancel भी हो सकती हैं — तो कभी shortcut मत मारिए।
Safe recipe हमेशा एक ही है: हर force को x और y components में resolve कीजिए, components को अलग-अलग जोड़िए।
फिर F net बराबर root of F x squared plus F y squared से recombine कीजिए, और direction पढ़ लीजिए।

board_events.text: Uniform spheres: use the point formula with centre-to-centre $r$.
Double $r$: since $F\propto 1/r^2$, the force falls to a quarter.
Even 200 kg of iron pulls feebly — gravity is tiny for us.

segments.text: A clean board-level warm-up. Two uniform iron spheres, eighty kilograms and one hundred twenty kilograms, with their centres half a metre apart. Find the force, and what happens if we double the distance.
Because both are uniform spheres, the shell theorem lets us treat each mass as concentrated at its centre, and use the point-mass formula directly.
So r is simply the centre-to-centre distance, half a metre — no integration needed here.
Plug in: big G, six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven, times eighty, times one hundred twenty, all over zero point five zero squared.
The top is six point four zero three times ten to the minus seven; divide by zero point two five to get two point five six times ten to the minus six newtons.
Now double the separation. Since force goes as one over r squared, doubling r divides the force by four.
So the new force is two point five six times ten to the minus six, over four, which is six point four zero times ten to the minus seven newtons.
<curious>Notice how minuscule that is — two hundred kilograms of iron, yet a pull smaller than a whisper. Gravity really is feeble at human scale.
एक साफ़ board-level warm-up। दो uniform iron spheres, अस्सी kilograms और एक सौ बीस kilograms, centres आधा metre दूर। force निकालिए, और अगर distance double कर दें तो क्या होगा।
चूँकि दोनों uniform spheres हैं, shell theorem हमें हर mass को उसके centre पर concentrated मानकर point-mass formula सीधे use करने देता है।
तो r बस centre-to-centre distance है, आधा metre — यहाँ कोई integration नहीं चाहिए।
Plug कीजिए: big G, six point six seven into ten to the minus eleven, into eighty, into one hundred twenty, सब कुछ zero point five zero squared के ऊपर।
ऊपर वाला है six point four zero three into ten to the minus seven; zero point two five से divide कीजिए तो मिलता है two point five six into ten to the minus six newtons।
अब separation double कीजिए। चूँकि force one over r squared के हिसाब से चलता है, r double करने पर force चार से divide हो जाता है।
तो नया force है two point five six into ten to the minus six, over four, यानी six point four zero into ten to the minus seven newtons।
<curious>ग़ौर कीजिए कितना छोटा है — दो सौ kilograms लोहा, फिर भी एक whisper से भी छोटा pull। gravity सच में human scale पर feeble है।

sections.title: Worked example: think in ratios, not numbers (NEET)

board_events.text: Triple one mass, halve the distance — new force?
The force between two point masses is $F_0$.
Tripling one mass multiplies $F$ by three.
Halving $r$: $r^2\to r^2/4$, so $F$ is multiplied by four.
Trap: the common wrong answer is $6F_0$ — distance enters as a SQUARE.

segments.text: This one is designed to be done in your head in ten seconds — if you respect the square.
We are told the force between two point masses is F naught. One mass is tripled and the distance between them is halved. Find the new force.
The whole trick is to think in ratios. Force is proportional to m one m two over r squared, so we can change each factor independently.
Tripling one mass multiplies the force by three. Straightforward.
Halving the distance is the sneaky part. Since r appears squared, halving r makes r squared one quarter, which multiplies the force by four.
Combine the two factors: three times four times F naught, which is twelve F naught.
<whisper>The classic trap is answering six F naught — three times two — forgetting that distance enters as a square, so halving it boosts the force by four, not two.
यह वाला दस second में दिमाग़ में करने के लिए बना है — बशर्ते आप square की इज़्ज़त करें।
हमें बताया गया है कि दो point masses के बीच force F naught है। एक mass triple कर दिया और उनके बीच distance आधा कर दिया। नया force निकालिए।
पूरी trick है ratios में सोचना। force, m one m two over r squared के proportional है, तो हम हर factor को अलग-अलग बदल सकते हैं।
एक mass triple करने से force three गुना हो जाता है। सीधा-सादा।
Distance आधा करना ही चालाक हिस्सा है। चूँकि r squared में आता है, r आधा करने पर r squared एक-चौथाई हो जाता है, जो force को four गुना कर देता है।
दोनों factors मिलाइए: three into four into F naught, यानी twelve F naught।
<whisper>Classic trap है six F naught लिखना — three into two — यह भूलकर कि distance square में आता है, तो उसे आधा करने पर force four गुना बढ़ता है, two नहीं।

sections.title: Worked example: orbital speed by dimensional analysis (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Find how orbital speed depends on G, M, r
Assume $v=k\,G^a M^b r^c$, with $k$ dimensionless.
Time powers: $-2a=-1\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12$.
Mass: $b-a=0\Rightarrow b=\tfrac12$; length: $3a+c=1\Rightarrow c=-\tfrac12$.
So $v\propto\sqrt{GM/r}$ — the form, with no equation of motion solved.
Full dynamics gives $k=1$; dimensions alone fix the shape.

segments.text: <curious>A cross-topic favourite: gravitation meeting dimensional analysis. We want how a satellite's orbital speed depends on big G, the planet's mass M, and the orbital radius r.
Assume a power-law relation: v equals some dimensionless constant k, times G to the a, M to the b, r to the c. Our job is to pin down a, b and c.
Write each quantity's dimensions. Speed is L T to the minus one; big G is M to the minus one L cubed T to the minus two; M is just mass; r is length.
Substitute and collect powers on the right: mass to the b minus a, length to the three a plus c, time to the minus two a.
Now match exponents on both sides. Time first: minus two a equals minus one, so a is one half.
Mass: b minus a equals zero, so b is also one half. Length: three a plus c equals one, giving c equals minus one half.
Put them back: v equals k times the square root of big G M over r.
So orbital speed is proportional to the square root of G M over r — and we found the form without solving a single equation of motion.
The full dynamical theory, equating gravity to the centripetal force, gives k equal to one; but dimensions alone already pinned the shape. That is the power being tested.
<curious>एक cross-topic favourite: gravitation की मुलाक़ात dimensional analysis से। हमें चाहिए कि एक satellite की orbital speed, big G, planet के mass M, और orbital radius r पर कैसे depend करती है।
एक power-law relation मान लीजिए: v बराबर कोई dimensionless constant k, into G to the a, M to the b, r to the c। हमारा काम है a, b और c को pin करना।
हर quantity के dimensions लिखिए। Speed है L T to the minus one; big G है M to the minus one L cubed T to the minus two; M बस mass है; r length है।
Substitute करके दाईं तरफ powers इकट्ठा कीजिए: mass to the b minus a, length to the three a plus c, time to the minus two a।
अब दोनों तरफ exponents match कीजिए। पहले time: minus two a बराबर minus one, तो a है one half।
Mass: b minus a बराबर zero, तो b भी one half। Length: three a plus c बराबर one, जिससे c बराबर minus one half।
इन्हें वापस रखिए: v बराबर k into square root of big G M over r।
तो orbital speed, big G M over r के square root के proportional है — और हमने यह form एक भी equation of motion हल किए बिना निकाल ली।
पूरी dynamical theory, gravity को centripetal force के बराबर रखकर, k को one देती है; पर dimensions ने अकेले ही shape pin कर दिया। यही वो power है जो test हो रही है।

board_events.text: Why not $GMm/r^2$? No single $r$: parts sit at different distances.
All pulls align, so add magnitudes; integrate $x$ from $a$ to $a+L$.
Far field: $a\gg L\Rightarrow F\approx GMm/a^2$ — a point again.

segments.text: Now a JEE Advanced favourite that shows exactly why the point-mass shortcut can fail. A thin uniform rod of mass M and length L lies along a line, and a point mass m sits on that same line, a distance a from the near end. Find the pull on m.
Look at the setup first. The rod stretches away from m, and every little slice of it lies at a different distance — the near end close, the far end further.
That is why we cannot write big G M m over r squared: there is no single r. Different parts of the rod are genuinely at different distances.
So build it from slices. Let the rod's linear mass density be lambda, equal to M over L. A slice of length dx has mass dm equal to lambda dx.
Being a tiny piece, that slice acts like a point mass. Its pull on m is big G m dm over x squared, which is big G m lambda dx over x squared, where x is the slice's distance from m.
Every slice pulls in the same direction, straight along the line, so we may add magnitudes — no vector resolution. We integrate x from a, the near end, to a plus L, the far end.
The integral of one over x squared gives minus one over x, so the force is big G m lambda times, one over a minus one over a plus L.
Substitute lambda equals M over L and tidy up: the force is big G M m over a times a plus L. Clean and closed-form.

<excited>Always sanity-check the far field. If a is much bigger than L, then a plus L is nearly a, and F collapses to big G M m over a squared — the rod looks like a point. If your limit fails that test, hunt down the error.

अब एक JEE Advanced favourite जो साफ़ दिखाता है कि point-mass shortcut कब fail होता है। mass M और length L का एक पतला uniform rod एक line पर पड़ा है, और उसी line पर एक point mass m, near end से distance a पर बैठा है। m पर pull निकालिए।
पहले setup देखिए। rod, m से दूर तक फैला है, और उसका हर छोटा slice अलग distance पर है — near end पास, far end दूर।
इसीलिए हम big G M m over r squared नहीं लिख सकते: कोई single r है ही नहीं। rod के अलग-अलग हिस्से सचमुच अलग distances पर हैं।
तो इसे slices से बनाइए। rod का linear mass density lambda मान लीजिए, बराबर M over L। length dx के एक slice का mass dm बराबर lambda dx है।
छोटा टुकड़ा होने से वो slice एक point mass की तरह act करता है। m पर इसका pull है big G m dm over x squared, यानी big G m lambda dx over x squared, जहाँ x उस slice की m से distance है।
हर slice एक ही direction में खींचता है, सीधे line के साथ, तो हम magnitudes जोड़ सकते हैं — कोई vector resolution नहीं। हम x को a, near end, से a plus L, far end, तक integrate करते हैं।
One over x squared का integral देता है minus one over x, तो force है big G m lambda into, one over a minus one over a plus L।
Lambda बराबर M over L रखिए और tidy कीजिए: force है big G M m over a into a plus L। साफ़ और closed-form।

<excited>Far field हमेशा sanity-check कीजिए। अगर a, L से बहुत बड़ा है, तो a plus L लगभग a है, और F सिमटकर big G M m over a squared बन जाता है — rod फिर एक point जैसा दिखता है। अगर आपका limit यह test fail करे, तो error ढूँढिए।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for Newton's law

board_events.text: Four traps and two time-savers
1. Forgetting the square: distance ×k changes force by $1/k^2$, not $1/k$.
2. Point formula on rods, rings, arcs — these need integration.
3. Adding force magnitudes, not vectors — resolve first.
4. Gravity is not electrostatics — no medium effect, no shielding, no repulsion.
Ask: is every part the same distance away? If not, integrate.
Pro-tip: solve by ratio — $F\propto m_1 m_2/r^2$.
Pro-tip: check the far field reduces to $GMm/r^2$.

segments.text: Let us close Part one by turning the common mistakes into a checklist, plus two tricks that save real time.
Trap one, the big one: forgetting the square. When distance changes by a factor k, the force changes by one over k squared, not one over k. Halving the distance quadruples the force.
Trap two: using big G M m over r squared on extended bodies. It is licensed only for point masses, uniform spheres, or a sphere and a point. Rods, rings and arcs demand integration.
Trap three: adding force magnitudes instead of vectors. Two pulls at an angle can partly cancel. Always resolve into components first.
Trap four: importing electrostatics. Gravity is always attractive, medium-independent, and cannot be shielded — so no dielectric constants, and no repulsion.
A single question defuses trap two instantly: is every part of this body the same distance from my particle? If not, you must integrate.
First time-saver: solve by ratio. For any what-happens-to-F question, write F proportional to m one m two over r squared and multiply the separate factors in your head.
<whisper>Second time-saver: after any extended-body integration, push the distance far beyond the body's size — the answer must reduce to big G M m over r squared, or you have slipped.
Part one को इन common mistakes को एक checklist में बदलकर ख़त्म करते हैं, साथ में दो tricks जो सचमुच time बचाती हैं।
Trap one, सबसे बड़ा: square भूल जाना। जब distance एक factor k से बदलता है, तो force one over k squared से बदलता है, one over k से नहीं। distance आधा करने पर force चार गुना।
Trap two: extended bodies पर big G M m over r squared use करना। यह सिर्फ़ point masses, uniform spheres, या एक sphere और एक point के लिए licensed है। rods, rings और arcs को integration चाहिए।
Trap three: vectors की जगह force magnitudes जोड़ना। एक angle पर दो pulls आंशिक रूप से cancel हो सकती हैं। हमेशा पहले components में resolve कीजिए।
Trap four: electrostatics import करना। gravity हमेशा attractive है, medium-independent है, और shield नहीं की जा सकती — तो कोई dielectric constants नहीं, कोई repulsion नहीं।
एक सवाल trap two को तुरंत ख़त्म कर देता है: क्या इस body का हर हिस्सा मेरे particle से एक ही distance पर है? अगर नहीं, तो integrate करना ही होगा।
पहली time-saver: ratio से हल कीजिए। किसी भी what-happens-to-F सवाल में, F को m one m two over r squared के proportional लिखिए और अलग-अलग factors को दिमाग़ में multiply कीजिए।
<whisper>दूसरी time-saver: किसी भी extended-body integration के बाद, distance को body के size से बहुत आगे धकेलिए — जवाब big G M m over r squared में सिमटना चाहिए, वरना कहीं चूक हुई है।

sections.title: From action-at-a-distance to the field picture

board_events.text: The field: gravity's middleman
Not 'Earth grabs the Moon' but 'Earth fills space with a field'.

board_events.text: Any mass dropped in feels a force set purely by the local field.
Units: N/kg = m/s$^2$ — the field IS the acceleration a free mass gets.
Put a 1 kg mass at the point; the force it feels is the field there.
The field exists at a point whether or not a mass is there to feel it.

segments.text: We began the chapter picturing gravity as a direct tug between two masses — action at a distance. Now meet a deeper way to see it, the way modern physics actually thinks.

Instead of saying the Earth reaches across empty space and grabs the Moon, we say the Earth fills the space around it with a gravitational field, and the Moon simply responds to the field right where it sits.
So how do we measure that field at a point? Place a one-kilogram test mass there, feel the gravitational force on it — that force, with its direction, is the field.
Every mass is a source that warps the space around it into a landscape of pulls. Any other mass dropped in feels a force set purely by the local field.
In symbols, the field E g equals the force F divided by the test mass m naught — force per kilogram.
Notice the units: newtons per kilogram, which is exactly metres per second squared. The field at a point literally is the acceleration a freely falling mass would have there.
That is the whole definition in one line: put a one-kilogram mass at the point, and the force it feels, direction included, is the gravitational field.
<curious>And the field is out there at every point, whether or not any mass is present to feel it — the middleman is always waiting.
Chapter की शुरुआत में हमने gravity को दो masses के बीच एक direct tug माना — action at a distance। अब इसे देखने का एक गहरा तरीक़ा, वही जिससे modern physics असल में सोचती है।

यह कहने के बजाय कि Earth खाली space के पार पहुँचकर Moon को पकड़ती है, हम कहते हैं कि Earth अपने चारों ओर की space को एक gravitational field से भर देती है, और Moon वहीं, जहाँ वो है, उस field को respond करता है।
तो उस field को किसी point पर कैसे measure करें? वहाँ एक one-kilogram test mass रखिए, उस पर gravitational force महसूस कीजिए — वही force, अपनी direction के साथ, वहाँ का field है।
हर mass एक source है जो अपने चारों ओर की space को pulls के एक landscape में warp कर देता है। उसमें गिराया कोई भी दूसरा mass, सिर्फ़ local field से तय एक force महसूस करता है।
Symbols में, field E g बराबर force F divided by test mass m naught — यानी force per kilogram।
Units ग़ौर कीजिए: newtons per kilogram, जो बिलकुल metres per second squared है। किसी point पर field सचमुच वही acceleration है जो एक freely falling mass को वहाँ मिलेगी।
यही पूरी definition एक line में: point पर एक one-kilogram mass रखिए, और उस पर लगने वाला force, direction समेत, gravitational field है।
<curious>और field हर point पर मौजूद है, चाहे उसे महसूस करने के लिए कोई mass हो या न हो — middleman हमेशा तैयार रहता है।

board_events.text: 9.8 m/s$^2$ is simply the Earth's field at its surface.
It exists at every point around the Earth — a landscape, not a number.
There whether or not anything feels it — that is what a field means.
So the g subtopic was secretly your first lesson in fields.
Generalise: every mass, not just the Earth, sets up a field.
And thanks to spheres, we can compute it cleanly for real bodies.

segments.text: Here is a reassuring surprise: you have already met a gravitational field intimately. It is called g.
The acceleration due to gravity, nine point eight metres per second squared, is nothing but the Earth's gravitational field at its surface, pointing inward everywhere.
When we said g is a property of the Earth and not of the falling object, we were really saying g is a field.
It exists at every point around the Earth, above the ground, on a mountain, out in orbit — a whole landscape of pulls, not a single number.
And crucially, it is there whether or not anything is present to feel it. That independence from any test mass is exactly what makes it a field.
So the earlier subtopic on g was, quietly, your very first lesson in fields — you just did not call it that.
Now we generalise. Every mass, not only the Earth, sets up such a field, and we can compute it for any shape we like.
<excited>And here is the payoff coming next: for spheres, the field takes an astonishingly clean form.
एक राहत भरी surprise: आप एक gravitational field से पहले ही अच्छी तरह मिल चुके हैं। उसका नाम है g।
Acceleration due to gravity, nine point eight metres per second squared, कुछ और नहीं बल्कि Earth का surface पर gravitational field है, जो हर तरफ अंदर की ओर point करता है।
जब हमने कहा कि g Earth की property है, गिरते object की नहीं, तो असल में हम कह रहे थे कि g एक field है।
यह Earth के चारों ओर हर point पर मौजूद है — ज़मीन के ऊपर, पहाड़ पर, orbit में — pulls का एक पूरा landscape, कोई एक number नहीं।
और अहम बात, यह वहाँ है चाहे उसे महसूस करने के लिए कोई हो या न हो। किसी test mass से यही आज़ादी इसे field बनाती है।
तो g वाला पिछला subtopic चुपके से fields का आपका पहला lesson था — आपने बस उसे यह नाम नहीं दिया।
अब generalise करते हैं। सिर्फ़ Earth ही नहीं, हर mass ऐसा field बनाता है, और हम इसे किसी भी shape के लिए compute कर सकते हैं।
<excited>और अगला payoff यह है: spheres के लिए field एक हैरान कर देने वाले साफ़ form में आता है।

board_events.text: Inside a uniform shell, the net field is ZERO everywhere.
Near patch: small but close. Far patch: large but distant. They cancel.
A solid planet is a stack of nested shells.
Outside it acts as a point; tunnelling in, the shells above you stop pulling.
Messy geometry becomes clean, layered simplicity.

segments.text: Why bother with the field picture at all? Because of one magical property of spheres that Newton proved — the shell theorem.
First half: a uniform spherical shell pulls any outside point exactly as if its entire mass were squeezed into a single point at the centre.
Second half is the surprising one. Take a point somewhere inside a uniform shell, off-centre.
The net field there is zero — everywhere inside, not just at the middle. Every pull is perfectly balanced.
Here is why. The nearby patch of shell is small but close; the far patch is large but distant. Closeness and largeness trade off so precisely that the two pulls cancel exactly.
Now build a solid planet as a stack of nested shells, one inside the next.
From outside, every shell acts like a point at the centre, so the whole planet does too. As you tunnel inward, each shell now above you contributes nothing.
<curious>That is the gift of the field picture: it turns messy geometry into clean, layered simplicity.
Field picture की ज़हमत क्यों उठाएँ? क्योंकि spheres की एक जादुई property है जिसे Newton ने साबित किया — shell theorem।
पहला हिस्सा: एक uniform spherical shell किसी बाहरी point को बिलकुल ऐसे खींचता है जैसे उसका पूरा mass centre पर एक single point में सिमट गया हो।
दूसरा हिस्सा चौंकाने वाला है। एक uniform shell के अंदर, centre से हटकर कोई point लीजिए।
वहाँ net field zero है — अंदर हर जगह, सिर्फ़ बीच में नहीं। हर pull पूरी तरह balanced है।
क्यों, देखिए। पास वाला patch छोटा पर क़रीब है; दूर वाला patch बड़ा पर दूर है। क़रीबी और बड़ाई इतनी सटीकता से trade-off करती हैं कि दोनों pulls बिलकुल cancel हो जाती हैं।
अब एक solid planet को nested shells के ढेर की तरह बनाइए, एक के अंदर दूसरा।
बाहर से हर shell centre पर एक point की तरह act करता है, तो पूरा planet भी वैसा ही। जैसे-जैसे आप अंदर सुरंग बनाते हैं, हर shell जो अब आपके ऊपर है, कुछ contribute नहीं करता।
<curious>यही field picture का तोहफ़ा है: यह messy geometry को साफ़, परतदार simplicity में बदल देता है।

board_events.text: Gravity only attracts, so lines only converge onto masses — never outward.
No negative mass, so no outgoing source lines exist.
Crowded lines = strong field; spread out = weak. Lines never cross.
A point mass: straight spokes pointing radially inward.
Two masses: lines merge, and at a null point none passes.
Sketch the lines and you know the force direction everywhere.

segments.text: We can even draw the field. Gravitational field lines are imaginary arrows pointing everywhere in the direction a test mass would be pushed.
So they always point inward, toward the source, like water draining toward a plughole.
Their rules mirror electric field lines, with one crucial difference. Gravity only attracts, so the lines only ever converge onto masses — never spray outward.
The reason is simple: there is no negative mass to repel anything, so there are no outgoing source lines at all.
Where the lines crowd together, near a mass, the field is strong; where they spread out, it is weak. And field lines never cross — at any point the field has one definite direction.
For a single point mass they are straight spokes, pointing radially inward from every direction.
For two masses they curve and merge, and at a null point, where the field vanishes, no line passes through at all.
<whisper>Sketching the lines is a fast sanity check: draw them, and you already know the direction of the force everywhere.
हम field को draw भी कर सकते हैं। gravitational field lines काल्पनिक arrows हैं जो हर जगह उस direction में point करती हैं जिधर एक test mass धकेला जाएगा।
तो वे हमेशा अंदर की ओर, source की तरफ point करती हैं, जैसे पानी किसी plughole की तरफ बहता है।
इनके rules electric field lines जैसे हैं, एक अहम फ़र्क़ के साथ। gravity सिर्फ़ attract करती है, तो lines हमेशा masses पर converge करती हैं — कभी बाहर की ओर नहीं फैलतीं।
वजह सीधी है: repel करने के लिए कोई negative mass है ही नहीं, तो कोई outgoing source lines होती ही नहीं।
जहाँ lines पास-पास होती हैं, mass के क़रीब, field strong है; जहाँ फैली होती हैं, weak। और field lines कभी cross नहीं करतीं — हर point पर field की एक ही definite direction होती है।
एक single point mass के लिए वे सीधी spokes हैं, हर दिशा से radially अंदर की ओर।
दो masses के लिए वे curve होकर merge होती हैं, और null point पर, जहाँ field ग़ायब हो जाता है, कोई line गुज़रती ही नहीं।
<whisper>Lines का sketch एक तेज़ sanity check है: उन्हें draw कीजिए, और आपको हर जगह force की direction पहले से पता है।

board_events.text: Derivation: on a test mass, $F=GMm_0/r^2$; divide by $m_0$.
The test mass cancels — the field belongs to the source and the location.
Dimensions $[E_g]=[LT^{-2}]$, like acceleration. Many sources add as vectors.
At the Earth's surface, $E_g=g$ — the same physical quantity.

segments.text: Time to put numbers on the field. Start with the simplest source, a point mass.
By definition the field is the force per unit test mass, E g equals F over m naught. For a point mass its magnitude is big G M over r squared, directed toward M.
Picture it as radial arrows pointing straight inward, strong near the mass and fading as one over r squared farther out.
The derivation is a single line. Put a test mass m naught at distance r; the force on it is big G M m naught over r squared. Now divide by m naught.
The test mass cancels, leaving E g equals big G M over r squared.
That cancellation carries a message: the field is a property of the source and the location, not of whatever tiny mass we use to probe it.
Its dimensions are L T to the minus two — identical to acceleration, as promised. And when several masses act, their fields add as vectors, not as bare numbers.
<curious>One more anchor: at the Earth's surface, E g equals g. Field intensity and acceleration due to gravity are the same physical quantity.
अब field पर numbers रखते हैं। सबसे आसान source से शुरू, एक point mass।
Definition से field, force per unit test mass है, E g बराबर F over m naught। एक point mass के लिए इसका magnitude है big G M over r squared, M की तरफ directed।
इसे radial arrows की तरह देखिए जो सीधे अंदर point करती हैं, mass के पास strong और दूर जाकर one over r squared के हिसाब से fade होती हुई।
Derivation एक ही line है। distance r पर एक test mass m naught रखिए; उस पर force है big G M m naught over r squared। अब m naught से divide कीजिए।
Test mass cancel हो जाता है, बचता है E g बराबर big G M over r squared।
वो cancellation एक message देता है: field, source और location की property है, उस छोटे mass की नहीं जिससे हम probe करते हैं।
इसके dimensions हैं L T to the minus two — acceleration जैसे ही, जैसा वादा था। और जब कई masses act करें, उनके fields vectors की तरह जुड़ते हैं, bare numbers की तरह नहीं।
<curious>एक और anchor: Earth के surface पर E g बराबर g। field intensity और acceleration due to gravity एक ही physical quantity हैं।

board_events.text: Split the ring into elements $dm$, each at distance $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ from P.
By symmetry, perpendicular parts of opposite elements cancel; keep the axial part.
Zero at the centre; far away it becomes $GM/x^2$ — a point again.
Setting $dE_g/dx=0$ gives the maximum field at $x=a/\sqrt{2}$.

segments.text: Now a shape JEE loves: a uniform ring, and the gravitational field along its axis, at a point P a distance x from the centre.
Look at the geometry first. Every tiny element of the ring sits at the same slant distance from P — the square root of a squared plus x squared.
Split the ring into little mass elements d m. Each one lies at that same distance, which is what makes the ring so friendly to handle.
Each element produces a field d E equal to big G d m over a squared plus x squared, pointing from P toward that element.
Now use symmetry. For every element there is a diametrically opposite one, and their perpendicular components cancel. Only the axial component survives.
That axial part is d E times cos theta, which works out to big G x d m over a squared plus x squared, all to the three halves.
Since x and a are the same for every element, we just integrate d m over the whole ring to get M. The field is big G M x over a squared plus x squared, to the three halves.
Check the ends. At the centre, x equals zero, the field is zero — every pull cancels its opposite. Far away, it reduces to big G M over x squared, the ring looking like a point.
<curious>And setting the derivative d E g by d x to zero gives a peak: the field is maximum at x equals a over root two.
अब एक shape जो JEE को बहुत पसंद है: एक uniform ring, और उसके axis के साथ gravitational field, centre से distance x पर एक point P पर।
पहले geometry देखिए। ring का हर छोटा element P से एक ही slant distance पर है — square root of a squared plus x squared।
Ring को छोटे mass elements d m में बाँटिए। हर एक उसी distance पर है, यही ring को handle करने में इतना friendly बनाता है।
हर element एक field d E पैदा करता है, बराबर big G d m over a squared plus x squared, जो P से उस element की तरफ point करता है।
अब symmetry use कीजिए। हर element के सामने एक diametrically opposite element है, और उनके perpendicular components cancel हो जाते हैं। सिर्फ़ axial component बचता है।
वो axial part है d E into cos theta, जो निकलता है big G x d m over a squared plus x squared, पूरा to the three halves।
चूँकि x और a हर element के लिए same हैं, हम बस d m को पूरे ring पर integrate करके M पा लेते हैं। field है big G M x over a squared plus x squared, to the three halves।
सिरे check कीजिए। centre पर, x बराबर zero, field zero है — हर pull अपने opposite से cancel। दूर, यह big G M over x squared बन जाता है, ring एक point जैसा दिखता है।
<curious>और derivative d E g by d x को zero रखने पर एक peak मिलता है: field, x बराबर a over root two पर maximum होता है।

board_events.text: Interior zero: near patch small-but-close, far patch large-but-distant — cancel.
Only mass enclosed within your radius pulls you: $M_{\text{enc}}=M\,r^3/R^3$.
Field–potential link: $E_g=-\,dV/dr$.

segments.text: Now the two results that generate almost every shell and sphere question — and the graphs that go with them.
Keep these two pictures in your head. For a shell, the field is flat zero inside, then jumps at the surface and decays. For a solid sphere, it rises in a straight line to the surface, then decays.
For a uniform shell: inside, the field is exactly zero; at the surface it is big G M over R squared; outside it is big G M over r squared, the point-mass value.
The zero inside is the shell theorem again: the near patch is small but close, the far patch large but distant, and they cancel perfectly.
For a solid sphere: inside, the field is big G M r over R cubed; outside, big G M over r squared, just like a point.
Why the inside form? Only the mass enclosed within your radius pulls you. That enclosed mass is M times r cubed over R cubed.
Put it into big G M enclosed over r squared, and the r-cubed over R-cubed simplifies to give big G M r over R cubed.
<whisper>And a bridge to the next subtopic: the field is the negative slope of the potential, E g equals minus d V by d r.
अब वो दो results जो लगभग हर shell और sphere सवाल पैदा करते हैं — और उनके साथ वाले graphs।
ये दो तस्वीरें दिमाग़ में रखिए। एक shell के लिए field अंदर flat zero है, फिर surface पर jump करके decay होता है। एक solid sphere के लिए यह surface तक सीधी line में उठता है, फिर decay होता है।
एक uniform shell के लिए: अंदर field बिलकुल zero; surface पर big G M over R squared; बाहर big G M over r squared, यानी point-mass value।
अंदर का zero फिर से shell theorem है: पास वाला patch छोटा पर क़रीब, दूर वाला बड़ा पर दूर, और वे पूरी तरह cancel।
एक solid sphere के लिए: अंदर field है big G M r over R cubed; बाहर big G M over r squared, बिलकुल एक point की तरह।
अंदर वाला form क्यों? सिर्फ़ आपके radius के अंदर घिरा mass आपको खींचता है। वो enclosed mass है M into r cubed over R cubed।
इसे big G M enclosed over r squared में रखिए, और r-cubed over R-cubed simplify होकर देता है big G M r over R cubed।
<whisper>और अगले subtopic का पुल: field, potential का negative slope है, E g बराबर minus d V by d r।

board_events.text: Masses 1.0 m apart. Let the null point be $x$ from the 4 kg mass.

segments.text: A clean board example on field cancellation. Two point masses, four kilograms and nine kilograms, are one metre apart. Where on the line between them is the net field zero?

Between the masses the two fields point toward opposite masses, so they can indeed cancel. Let the null point be a distance x from the four-kilogram mass, and therefore one minus x from the nine-kilogram one.
Set the two field magnitudes equal — that is the whole condition for a null point.
Big G times four over x squared equals big G times nine over one minus x squared. The big G cancels, leaving four over x squared equals nine over one minus x squared.
Now take square roots of both sides. Between the masses both distances are positive, so we may do this cleanly.
Two over x equals three over one minus x. Cross-multiply: two times one minus x equals three x.
That gives two equals five x, so x is zero point four metres, and one minus x is zero point six.
<curious>Notice the null point lies closer to the smaller mass. That is always true, and it is a quick way to sanity-check your answer.
Field cancellation पर एक साफ़ board example। दो point masses, चार kilograms और नौ kilograms, एक metre दूर हैं। उनके बीच line पर net field कहाँ zero है?
Masses के बीच दोनों fields opposite masses की तरफ point करती हैं, तो वे सचमुच cancel हो सकती हैं। null point को चार-kilogram mass से distance x पर लीजिए, यानी नौ-kilogram से one minus x पर।
दोनों field magnitudes को बराबर रखिए — null point की यही पूरी condition है।
Big G into four over x squared बराबर big G into nine over one minus x squared। big G cancel, बचता है four over x squared बराबर nine over one minus x squared।
अब दोनों तरफ square roots लीजिए। masses के बीच दोनों distances positive हैं, तो हम यह साफ़ कर सकते हैं।
Two over x बराबर three over one minus x। cross-multiply: two into one minus x बराबर three x।
इससे मिलता है two बराबर five x, तो x है zero point four metres, और one minus x है zero point six।
<curious>ग़ौर कीजिए null point छोटे mass के क़रीब है। यह हमेशा सच है, और जवाब को sanity-check करने का एक तेज़ तरीक़ा है।

board_events.text: Think in cases — no calculation needed.
At the centre: the shell gives $E=0$ (interior of a shell).
So both are zero at the centre.
They differ only inside: shell 0 throughout, solid rises linearly.

segments.text: A NEET-style thinking problem, solvable entirely in cases. A hollow shell and a solid sphere have the same mass M and the same radius R. Where is the field zero, and where is it identical for both?
Keep the comparison picture in mind: the two agree at the centre and at the surface, and differ only in between.
No calculation is really needed — just reason case by case.
At the centre, the shell gives zero, because the field is zero everywhere inside a shell.
The solid sphere also gives zero at its centre: its interior field is big G M r over R cubed, and at r equals zero that is zero too.
So both bodies give zero field at the centre. That is the first meeting point.
At the surface, r equals R, both give big G M over R squared — because from the surface outward, any spherically symmetric mass M looks exactly like a point mass.

<whisper>The trap is thinking the solid sphere has a non-zero field at its centre, or that the two differ at the surface. They differ only inside: zero throughout the shell, linearly rising inside the solid.
एक NEET-style thinking problem, जो पूरी तरह cases में हल होती है। एक hollow shell और एक solid sphere का same mass M और same radius R है। field कहाँ zero है, और कहाँ दोनों के लिए एक जैसा है?
Comparison तस्वीर याद रखिए: दोनों centre और surface पर agree करते हैं, और सिर्फ़ बीच में differ करते हैं।
असल में कोई calculation नहीं चाहिए — बस case दर case reason कीजिए।
Centre पर, shell zero देता है, क्योंकि shell के अंदर हर जगह field zero है।
Solid sphere भी अपने centre पर zero देता है: इसका interior field big G M r over R cubed है, और r बराबर zero पर वह भी zero है।
तो दोनों bodies centre पर zero field देते हैं। यह पहला meeting point है।
Surface पर, r बराबर R, दोनों big G M over R squared देते हैं — क्योंकि surface से बाहर, कोई भी spherically symmetric mass M बिलकुल एक point mass जैसा दिखता है।
<whisper>Trap यह सोचना है कि solid sphere के centre पर non-zero field है, या दोनों surface पर differ करते हैं। वे सिर्फ़ अंदर differ करते हैं: shell में हर जगह zero, solid में linearly बढ़ता हुआ।

board_events.text: Differentiate with respect to $x$ and set to zero.
Substitute back, using $a^2+x^2=\tfrac{3a^2}{2}$.
Zero at the centre, this peak, then decay — a shape JEE loves.

segments.text: A JEE Main favourite: find the axial distance where a ring's gravitational field is maximum, and the value of that maximum.
The profile is non-monotonic: the field starts at zero at the centre, climbs to a single peak, then decays. We want that peak.
Start from the axial field, big G M x over a squared plus x squared, all to the three halves.
To maximise, differentiate with respect to x and set the derivative to zero.
After differentiating, the numerator gives a squared plus x squared minus three x squared equals zero.
That simplifies to a squared equals two x squared, so x equals a over root two — the location of the peak.
Now substitute back. At this x, a squared plus x squared equals three a squared over two, which we raise to the three halves.
Carefully simplified, the maximum field is two big G M over three root three a squared, about zero point three eight five times big G M over a squared.
<curious>So it is zero at the centre, rises to this peak at a over root two, then decays — exactly the non-monotonic shape examiners love to probe.
एक JEE Main favourite: वो axial distance निकालिए जहाँ एक ring का gravitational field maximum है, और उस maximum की value।
Profile non-monotonic है: field centre पर zero से शुरू होता है, एक single peak तक चढ़ता है, फिर decay करता है। हमें वही peak चाहिए।
Axial field से शुरू कीजिए, big G M x over a squared plus x squared, पूरा to the three halves।
Maximise करने के लिए, x के respect में differentiate कीजिए और derivative को zero रखिए।
Differentiate के बाद, numerator देता है a squared plus x squared minus three x squared बराबर zero।
यह simplify होकर a squared बराबर two x squared, तो x बराबर a over root two — peak की जगह।
अब वापस substitute कीजिए। इस x पर, a squared plus x squared बराबर three a squared over two, जिसे हम to the three halves उठाते हैं।
ध्यान से simplify करने पर, maximum field है two big G M over three root three a squared, लगभग zero point three eight five into big G M over a squared।
<curious>तो यह centre पर zero है, a over root two पर इस peak तक चढ़ता है, फिर decay करता है — बिलकुल वही non-monotonic shape जिसे examiners probe करना पसंद करते हैं।

board_events.text: Cavity radius $R/2$, centre at $R/2$ from the sphere's centre.
The point P cancels — the result does not depend on where you are inside.
Uniform field everywhere in the hollow — a signature JEE Advanced result.

segments.text: Now a signature JEE Advanced result. A solid uniform sphere of density rho has a spherical cavity of radius R over two scooped out, with the cavity's centre a distance R over two from the sphere's centre. Show the field inside the cavity is uniform, and find it.
The whole trick is superposition. A sphere with a cavity is the same as a complete solid sphere, minus a small solid sphere that would exactly fill the hole.
So the field at any point inside the cavity is the field of the full sphere minus the field of that imaginary small sphere.
We need one fact: for a point inside a uniform solid sphere, the interior field is minus four thirds pi big G rho, times the position vector from that sphere's own centre.
Write it for both spheres and subtract. The field in the cavity is minus four thirds pi G rho, times r from O minus r from O prime — but that difference is just the vector d joining the two centres.
Watch what vanished: the point P cancelled out completely. The field does not depend on where inside the cavity you are — it is the same everywhere.
Its magnitude is four thirds pi G rho times R over two, which is two thirds pi G rho R, directed along the line of centres toward the big sphere's centre.
<excited>Every point in the hollow feels the identical pull — a perfectly uniform field, one of the most elegant consequences of the inverse-square law.

अब एक signature JEE Advanced result। density rho के एक solid uniform sphere में से radius R over two की एक spherical cavity निकाली गई है, cavity का centre sphere के centre से R over two की दूरी पर। दिखाइए कि cavity के अंदर field uniform है, और उसे निकालिए।
पूरी trick superposition है। cavity वाला sphere वही है जो एक complete solid sphere, minus एक छोटा solid sphere जो hole को बिलकुल भर दे।
तो cavity के अंदर किसी भी point पर field, full sphere के field minus उस काल्पनिक छोटे sphere के field के बराबर है।
हमें एक fact चाहिए: एक uniform solid sphere के अंदर किसी point के लिए, interior field है minus four thirds pi big G rho, into उस sphere के अपने centre से position vector।
इसे दोनों spheres के लिए लिखकर घटाइए। cavity में field है minus four thirds pi G rho, into r from O minus r from O prime — पर वो difference बस दोनों centres को जोड़ने वाला vector d है।
देखिए क्या ग़ायब हुआ: point P पूरी तरह cancel हो गया। field इस पर depend नहीं करता कि आप cavity के अंदर कहाँ हैं — यह हर जगह same है।
इसका magnitude है four thirds pi G rho into R over two, यानी two thirds pi G rho R, centres की line के साथ big sphere के centre की तरफ directed।
<excited>Hollow का हर point एक जैसा pull महसूस करता है — एक बिलकुल uniform field, inverse-square law के सबसे elegant नतीजों में से एक।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for gravitational field

board_events.text: Field: the traps and the shortcuts
1. Shell vs solid inside: shell $E=0$ everywhere; solid $E=GMr/R^3$ rises.
2. Field is a VECTOR — equal opposite fields cancel; resolve into components.
3. Zero field ≠ zero potential: inside a shell $E=0$ but $V=-GM/R$.
4. Only enclosed mass pulls you inside a sphere — outer shells do nothing.
Sketch the E–r graph before answering shell/sphere questions.
Pro-tip: uniform-sphere interior $\vec{E}=-\tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho\,\vec{r}$ — cavities fall out.
Pro-tip: outside = point mass; inside = enclosed mass only.

segments.text: Let us close Part two with the field traps and the shortcuts that beat them.

Trap one: confusing a shell with a solid sphere inside. Inside a shell the field is zero everywhere; inside a solid sphere it rises linearly as big G M r over R cubed. Draw the wrong E–r graph and you lose easy marks.
Trap two: adding field magnitudes instead of vectors. Field is a vector, so two equal fields in opposite directions cancel. Always resolve into components first.

Trap three, the deep one: assuming zero field means zero potential. Inside a shell the field is zero, yet the potential is a non-zero constant, minus big G M over R. Field is the slope of potential, not its value.
Trap four: forgetting the enclosed-mass rule. Inside a sphere, only the mass within your own radius pulls you; the outer shells contribute nothing at all.
One habit prevents most of these: sketch the E versus r graph before you answer any shell or sphere question. The picture settles inside-versus-outside instantly.
First pro-tip: for any uniform-sphere interior, the field is minus four thirds pi big G rho times the position vector. That single line cracks every cavity problem by superposition.
<whisper>Second pro-tip: for symmetric bodies, think outside equals point mass, inside equals enclosed mass only. That converts nearly every shell or sphere question into a one-line answer.
Part two को field के traps और उन्हें हराने वाले shortcuts के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं।

Trap one: shell को solid sphere के अंदर से confuse करना। shell के अंदर field हर जगह zero है; solid sphere के अंदर यह linearly बढ़ता है, big G M r over R cubed। ग़लत E–r graph draw किया तो आसान marks गए।
Trap two: vectors की जगह field magnitudes जोड़ना। field एक vector है, तो opposite directions में दो बराबर fields cancel हो जाती हैं। हमेशा पहले components में resolve कीजिए।

Trap three, गहरा वाला: यह मानना कि zero field का मतलब zero potential है। shell के अंदर field zero है, फिर भी potential एक non-zero constant है, minus big G M over R। field, potential का slope है, उसकी value नहीं।
Trap four: enclosed-mass rule भूलना। एक sphere के अंदर, सिर्फ़ आपके अपने radius के अंदर वाला mass आपको खींचता है; बाहरी shells बिलकुल कुछ contribute नहीं करतीं।
एक आदत इनमें से ज़्यादातर रोक देती है: किसी भी shell या sphere सवाल का जवाब देने से पहले E versus r graph sketch कीजिए। तस्वीर inside-versus-outside तुरंत तय कर देती है।
पहली pro-tip: किसी भी uniform-sphere interior के लिए, field है minus four thirds pi big G rho into position vector। यही एक line superposition से हर cavity problem को crack कर देती है।
<whisper>दूसरी pro-tip: symmetric bodies के लिए सोचिए outside बराबर point mass, inside बराबर सिर्फ़ enclosed mass। यह लगभग हर shell या sphere सवाल को one-line answer में बदल देता है।

  <text x="146" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#b3402f">g</text>
  <text x="326" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#b3402f">g</text>
  <line x1="55" y1="196" x2="395" y2="196" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="225" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#2f7d5a">bigger pull AND harder to move → a = F/m = g, the same for both</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A feather and a hammer, in no air, hit the ground together.
The Earth pulls harder on heavier mass ($F=GMm/R^2$)...
...but heavier mass resists more — so in $g=F/m$ the mass cancels.
The pull and the sluggishness scale together and balance.
So g is a property of the Earth, not of the falling object.

segments.text: This subtopic asks a sharper question than before: if I let go of something, how fast does gravity make it speed up? That rate is the acceleration due to gravity, written g.
Near the Earth's surface it is about nine point eight metres per second squared, meaning a dropped stone gets nine point eight metres per second faster with every passing second.
Here is the most beautiful fact about g: it does not care what you drop. A cricket ball and a crumpled sheet, a feather and a hammer — with no air, they all accelerate at the same g.
Astronaut David Scott famously showed this on the Moon, releasing a hammer and a feather that landed together. Why does it happen?
Because the Earth pulls harder on a heavier object — bigger m means bigger force, big G M m over R squared.
But that same heavier object is also harder to accelerate. When you compute g as force over mass, the object's mass cancels completely.
The strength of the pull and the sluggishness of the mass scale together, and they balance perfectly, leaving one common g.
<curious>So g is a property of the Earth — its mass and radius — not of whatever happens to be falling.
यह subtopic पहले से एक तेज़ सवाल पूछता है: अगर मैं कुछ छोड़ूँ, तो gravity उसे कितनी तेज़ी से speed up कराती है? वो rate है acceleration due to gravity, जिसे g लिखते हैं।
Earth के surface के पास यह लगभग nine point eight metres per second squared है, यानी एक गिरता पत्थर हर गुज़रते second के साथ nine point eight metres per second तेज़ हो जाता है।
g के बारे में सबसे ख़ूबसूरत fact: इसे परवाह नहीं कि आप क्या गिराते हैं। एक cricket ball और एक मुड़ा काग़ज़, एक feather और एक hammer — बिना हवा के, सब एक ही g से accelerate होते हैं।
Astronaut David Scott ने मशहूर तौर पर यह Moon पर दिखाया, एक hammer और एक feather छोड़े जो साथ गिरे। ऐसा क्यों होता है?
क्योंकि Earth एक भारी object को ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींचती है — बड़ा m यानी बड़ा force, big G M m over R squared।
पर वही भारी object accelerate होने में भी ज़्यादा मुश्किल है। जब आप g को force over mass निकालते हैं, object का mass पूरी तरह cancel हो जाता है।
Pull की ताक़त और mass की सुस्ती साथ-साथ scale करती हैं, और पूरी तरह balance हो जाती हैं, एक common g छोड़कर।
<curious>तो g Earth की property है — उसके mass और radius की — न कि गिरते किसी object की।

sections.title: Computing g, and how it changes from place to place

board_events.text: Setting weight equal to the gravitational pull
The mass $m$ vanishes — g depends only on the Earth's $M$ and $R$.

board_events.caption: g weakens going up, going down, and toward the equator

</svg>

board_events.text: Go up a mountain or into orbit: farther from the centre, so g decreases.
Go down a mine: the shell now above you stops pulling, so g decreases.
Toward the equator: the spin and the bulge both make g smaller.
So g is greatest right at the surface, near the poles.

segments.text: How do we actually compute g? The Earth's pull on a surface object equals that object's weight, m g. So set Newton's law equal to the weight.
Big G M m over R squared equals m g. The little mass m appears on both sides.
Cancel it, and g equals big G M over R squared. The falling body's mass has vanished — exactly as our intuition demanded. g depends only on the Earth's mass and radius.
But g is not a single frozen number. It changes with where you stand, and the picture shows the three ways.
Go up — a mountain, an aircraft, orbit — and you are farther from the Earth's centre, so g decreases.
Go down into a mine, and surprisingly g also decreases, because the shell of Earth now above you stops pulling you down.
Move toward the equator, and two things shrink g: the Earth's spin flings you outward slightly, and the equatorial bulge puts you farther from the centre.
<curious>So g is maximum right at the surface near the poles, and tapers off as you climb up, dig down, or drift toward the equator.
g असल में कैसे compute करें? Earth का surface object पर pull, उस object के weight m g के बराबर है। तो Newton के law को weight के बराबर रखिए।
Big G M m over R squared बराबर m g। छोटा mass m दोनों तरफ आता है।
इसे cancel कीजिए, और g बराबर big G M over R squared। गिरते body का mass ग़ायब हो गया — बिलकुल जैसा हमारी intuition ने माँगा। g सिर्फ़ Earth के mass और radius पर depend करता है।
पर g कोई एक जमा हुआ number नहीं है। यह इस पर बदलता है कि आप कहाँ खड़े हैं, और तस्वीर तीनों तरीक़े दिखाती है।
ऊपर जाइए — पहाड़, aircraft, orbit — और आप Earth के centre से दूर हैं, तो g घटता है।
एक mine में नीचे जाइए, और हैरानी की बात, g भी घटता है, क्योंकि Earth का shell जो अब आपके ऊपर है, आपको नीचे खींचना बंद कर देता है।
Equator की तरफ बढ़िए, और दो चीज़ें g को छोटा करती हैं: Earth का spin आपको थोड़ा बाहर फेंकता है, और equatorial bulge आपको centre से दूर रखता है।
<curious>तो g surface पर poles के पास maximum है, और जैसे-जैसे आप ऊपर चढ़ते, नीचे खोदते, या equator की तरफ बढ़ते हैं, कम होता जाता है।

sections.title: Gravity cannot be shielded — and g is the field

board_events.text: No Faraday cage for gravity
Seal a charge in a hollow metal box and the electric field inside vanishes.

board_events.text: There is no such trick for gravity.
You cannot block, absorb, or screen gravity with any material or shell.
Electricity has opposite charges to damp the field; gravity has no opposite.
Wherever there is mass, its gravity reaches through everything.
g at any point is numerically the gravitational field strength there.

segments.text: One more thing worth knowing, and examiners love it as a one-liner: gravity cannot be switched off.
You can shield a charge from an electric field by sealing it inside a hollow metal box — a Faraday cage. The field inside completely vanishes.
But there is no such trick for gravity. Put a cage around something and the electric field stops at the walls, while gravity sails straight through, untouched.
You simply cannot block, absorb, or screen the gravitational influence of nearby matter by wrapping an object in any material or hollow shell.
The reason is twofold: gravity is independent of the intervening medium, and there is no negative mass to cancel it.
Contrast that with electricity, where opposite charges and dielectrics let you damp or redirect the field. Gravity has no opposite.
So wherever there is mass, its gravity reaches through everything else in the way.
<curious>And this is also why g at any point is numerically identical to the gravitational field strength there — g is simply the field the Earth sets up, felt as an acceleration.
एक और जानने लायक़ बात, और examiners इसे one-liner के तौर पर पसंद करते हैं: gravity को बंद नहीं किया जा सकता।
आप एक charge को electric field से बचा सकते हैं, उसे एक hollow metal box में सील करके — एक Faraday cage। अंदर का field पूरी तरह ग़ायब हो जाता है।
पर gravity के लिए ऐसी कोई trick नहीं। किसी चीज़ के चारों ओर cage लगाइए और electric field दीवारों पर रुक जाता है, जबकि gravity सीधे, बिना छुए गुज़र जाती है।
आप किसी object को किसी भी material या hollow shell में लपेटकर आसपास के matter की gravitational influence को block, absorb, या screen कर ही नहीं सकते।
वजह दो तरफ़ा है: gravity बीच के medium से independent है, और इसे cancel करने के लिए कोई negative mass नहीं है।
इसकी तुलना electricity से कीजिए, जहाँ opposite charges और dielectrics आपको field को damp या redirect करने देते हैं। gravity का कोई opposite नहीं।
तो जहाँ भी mass है, उसकी gravity रास्ते में आने वाली हर चीज़ के आर-पार पहुँचती है।
<curious>और इसीलिए किसी भी point पर g, वहाँ की gravitational field strength के numerically बराबर है — g बस वो field है जो Earth बनाती है, एक acceleration की तरह महसूस होता।

sections.title: Surface g: the mass form and the density form

board_events.text: g at the surface, two useful forms

board_events.caption: Weight equals the gravitational pull, so mass cancels
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <defs><marker id="c4" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 Z" fill="#b3402f"/></marker></defs>
  <circle cx="150" cy="150" r="90" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="150" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">M, R</text>
  <rect x="140" y="48" width="20" height="14" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="176" y="56" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">m</text>
  <line x1="150" y1="64" x2="150" y2="118" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#c4)"/>
  <text x="330" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#2b6ca3">m g = GM m / R^2</text>
  <text x="330" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#2b6ca3">g = GM / R^2</text>
  <text x="330" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">the mass m cancels</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Treat the planet as a uniform sphere: all its mass acts as if at the centre.
The density form uses $M=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho$: at equal density, $g\propto R$.
Dimensions $[g]=[LT^{-2}]$; g is a vector, toward the centre.
g is independent of the mass, size, shape, and composition of the body.

segments.text: Let us lock down the surface value and a second form that saves time in comparison problems.

Picture a body resting on a planet of mass M and radius R. Treating the planet as a uniform sphere, its entire mass acts as if concentrated at the centre, so the pull is big G M m over R squared. That pull is the weight, m g.
Equate them and cancel the body's mass: g equals big G M over R squared. This is the value you will use by default.
It is worth pausing on the assumption: the shell theorem is what lets us pretend all the planet's mass sits at its centre.
Now a second, handier form. Write the mass as four thirds pi R cubed rho, and g becomes four thirds pi big G R rho.
This density form is powerful for comparisons: for planets of the same density, g is simply proportional to R — bigger planet, stronger surface gravity.
Its dimensions are L T to the minus two, and remember g is a vector, always pointing toward the planet's centre.
<whisper>And say it once for the exam: g is independent of the mass, size, shape, and composition of the falling body.
आइए surface value और एक दूसरा form पक्का करें जो comparison problems में time बचाता है।

एक body को mass M और radius R के planet पर रखा सोचिए। planet को uniform sphere मानते हुए, उसका पूरा mass centre पर concentrated जैसा act करता है, तो pull है big G M m over R squared। वो pull ही weight है, m g।
इन्हें बराबर रखकर body का mass cancel कीजिए: g बराबर big G M over R squared। यही value आप default में use करेंगे।
Assumption पर रुकना ज़रूरी है: shell theorem ही हमें planet का पूरा mass उसके centre पर मान लेने देता है।
अब एक दूसरा, ज़्यादा handy form। mass को four thirds pi R cubed rho लिखिए, और g बन जाता है four thirds pi big G R rho।
यह density form comparisons के लिए ताक़तवर है: एक ही density के planets के लिए, g सीधे R के proportional है — बड़ा planet, ज़्यादा surface gravity।
इसके dimensions हैं L T to the minus two, और याद रखिए g एक vector है, हमेशा planet के centre की तरफ point करता।
<whisper>और exam के लिए एक बार कह दीजिए: g गिरते body के mass, size, shape, और composition से independent है।

board_events.text: How g falls as you rise

board_events.caption: Exact curve versus the straight small-height approximation

  <line x1="55" y1="200" x2="55" y2="40" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="424" y="217" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">h</text>
  <text x="40" y="48" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">g</text>
  <path d="M55,70 Q170,150 420,188" fill="none" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.4"/>
  <line x1="55" y1="70" x2="245" y2="180" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="150" y="95" font-size="11.5" fill="#2f7d5a">exact: g R^2/(R+h)^2</text>
  <text x="150" y="150" font-size="11.5" fill="#b3402f">approx: g(1 minus 2h/R)</text>
  <text x="240" y="245" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">the straight approx only holds for small h</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: From outside, the planet is still a point at its centre — replace $R$ by $R+h$.
For small $h$: the factor is $2h/R$, so g falls TWICE as fast per unit height.
A 1% rise in altitude drops g by about 2%.
For satellites, $h$ is comparable to $R$ — use the full inverse-square form.

segments.text: Now watch how g weakens as you climb. At height h, the body is a distance R plus h from the centre.
The graph tells the whole story: the true fall of g is a smooth curve, while the familiar shortcut is only a straight tangent that hugs it near the ground.
The exact value is big G M over R plus h squared, which we can write as g divided by one plus h over R, all squared.
The reasoning is simple. From outside, the planet still behaves as a point mass at its centre, so we just replace R by R plus h in the surface formula.
When h is much smaller than R, the binomial approximation gives g h is about g times one minus two h over R.
Read that carefully: the factor is two h over R, not h over R. So g falls twice as fast per unit height as a naive guess would say.
Concretely, a one percent rise in altitude drops g by about two percent.
<whisper>The linear shortcut is trustworthy only for small h. For a satellite, where h is comparable to R or larger, it fails badly — use the full inverse-square form.
अब देखिए g कैसे weak होता है जब आप चढ़ते हैं। height h पर, body centre से R plus h दूरी पर है।
Graph पूरी कहानी कहता है: g का असली गिरना एक smooth curve है, जबकि जाना-पहचाना shortcut सिर्फ़ एक straight tangent है जो ज़मीन के पास उससे चिपकी रहती है।
Exact value है big G M over R plus h squared, जिसे हम g divided by one plus h over R, पूरा squared लिख सकते हैं।
Reasoning सीधी है। बाहर से, planet अब भी centre पर एक point mass की तरह behave करता है, तो हम surface formula में बस R को R plus h से बदल देते हैं।
जब h, R से बहुत छोटा हो, binomial approximation देता है g h लगभग g into one minus two h over R।
इसे ध्यान से पढ़िए: factor है two h over R, h over R नहीं। तो g per unit height दोगुनी तेज़ी से गिरता है, जितना एक naive guess कहेगा।
ठोस रूप में, altitude में एक percent की बढ़त g को लगभग two percent गिरा देती है।
<whisper>Linear shortcut सिर्फ़ छोटे h के लिए भरोसेमंद है। एक satellite के लिए, जहाँ h, R के comparable या बड़ा है, यह बुरी तरह fail होता है — पूरा inverse-square form use कीजिए।
