</svg>

board_events.text: A geostationary satellite sits about 36000 km up, in the equatorial plane.
It circles once every 24 hours, the same way the Earth spins.
So it hovers over one fixed spot — perfect for TV, phone, and weather relay.
A polar satellite orbits low, around 1000 km, in a north–south plane over the poles.
As the Earth turns beneath it, each pass scans a fresh strip of the surface.
High-and-fixed for communication; low-and-sweeping for imaging.

segments.text: Not all satellites are alike. Two special kinds are worth knowing precisely, because exams contrast them.
The figure shows the two orbits: one far out in the equatorial plane, one low and passing over the poles.
A geostationary satellite sits far out, about thirty-six thousand kilometres up, in the equatorial plane.
It circles the Earth once every twenty-four hours, in the same direction the Earth spins.
So from the ground it appears motionless, hovering over one fixed spot. That makes it perfect for television, telephone, and weather relay — your dish can point at one unchanging place.
A polar satellite is the opposite. It orbits low, around one thousand kilometres, in a north-south plane that passes over the poles.
As the Earth rotates beneath it, the satellite scans a fresh strip of the surface on each pass, eventually covering the whole globe.
<whisper>Remember it as a slogan: high-and-fixed for communication, low-and-sweeping for imaging and remote sensing.
सभी satellites एक जैसे नहीं होते। दो ख़ास किस्में सटीक जानने लायक़ हैं, क्योंकि exams इनकी तुलना करते हैं।
Figure दो orbits दिखाता है: एक equatorial plane में दूर, एक नीची और poles के ऊपर से गुज़रती।
एक geostationary satellite दूर बैठता है, लगभग छत्तीस हज़ार kilometres ऊपर, equatorial plane में।
यह Earth के चारों ओर हर चौबीस घंटे में एक बार घूमता है, उसी दिशा में जिधर Earth घूमती है।
तो ज़मीन से यह गतिहीन दिखता है, एक fixed spot पर मँडराता। यह इसे television, telephone, और weather relay के लिए perfect बनाता है — आपकी dish एक न बदलने वाली जगह पर point कर सकती है।
एक polar satellite उल्टा है। यह नीचे orbit करता है, लगभग एक हज़ार kilometres, एक north-south plane में जो poles के ऊपर से गुज़रती है।
जैसे Earth इसके नीचे घूमती है, satellite हर pass पर surface की एक ताज़ा पट्टी scan करता है, आख़िरकार पूरे globe को cover करते हुए।
<whisper>इसे एक नारे की तरह याद रखिए: communication के लिए high-and-fixed, imaging और remote sensing के लिए low-and-sweeping।

sections.title: Orbital velocity: gravity as the centripetal force

board_events.text: The speed that keeps a satellite in a circle

board_events.caption: The planet's pull is exactly the centripetal force needed
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 320" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <defs>
    <marker id="e5g" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 Z" fill="#2f7d5a"/></marker>
    <marker id="e5r" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 Z" fill="#b3402f"/></marker>
  </defs>
  <circle cx="185" cy="170" r="118" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <circle cx="185" cy="170" r="42" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="185" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">M</text>
  <circle cx="303" cy="170" r="11" fill="#2b6ca3"/>
  <line x1="303" y1="158" x2="303" y2="90" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#e5g)"/>
  <text x="310" y="112" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">v (tangent)</text>
  <line x1="290" y1="170" x2="234" y2="170" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#e5r)"/>
  <text x="250" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#b3402f">gravity</text>
  <text x="200" y="308" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r  →  v_o = √(GM/r)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: The only force is gravity, pointing inward — exactly what a circle needs.
The satellite's mass cancels — a bolt and a station orbit at the same speed.
Smaller orbits demand higher speeds: $v_o\propto 1/\sqrt{r}$.
Near the surface, $v_o=\sqrt{gR}\approx 7.9$ km/s.

segments.text: Now the speed a satellite must have to hold a circular orbit of radius r. Gravity does the whole job.
The only force on the satellite is the planet's gravity, pointing toward the centre — and that is exactly what a circular path needs as its centripetal force.
So the planet's pull does not fight the motion; it bends it into a circle. Set the gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force.
That is big G M m over r squared equals m v o squared over r.
Cancel m and one power of r, and the orbital velocity is the square root of big G M over r.
Notice the satellite's mass cancelled out. A single bolt and a whole space station at the same height orbit at exactly the same speed.
And smaller orbits demand higher speeds, since v o goes as one over root r — the closer in, the faster you must move.
<whisper>Near the surface, where r is about R, the orbital speed is root g R, roughly seven point nine kilometres per second.
अब वो speed जो एक satellite को radius r की circular orbit टिकाने के लिए चाहिए। gravity पूरा काम करती है।
Satellite पर एकमात्र force planet की gravity है, centre की तरफ point करती — और यही एक circular path को centripetal force के तौर पर चाहिए।
तो planet का pull motion से नहीं लड़ता; यह उसे एक circle में मोड़ता है। gravitational force को ज़रूरी centripetal force के बराबर रखिए।
यानी big G M m over r squared बराबर m v o squared over r।
m और r की एक power cancel कीजिए, और orbital velocity है square root of big G M over r।
ग़ौर कीजिए satellite का mass cancel हो गया। एक अकेला bolt और एक पूरा space station एक ही height पर बिलकुल एक ही speed से orbit करते हैं।
और छोटी orbits ज़्यादा speeds माँगती हैं, क्योंकि v o, one over root r के हिसाब से चलता है — जितना अंदर, उतना तेज़ चलना होगा।
<whisper>Surface के पास, जहाँ r लगभग R है, orbital speed है root g R, क़रीब seven point nine kilometres per second।

sections.title: Time period and Kepler's third law

board_events.text: One circumference per period

board_events.caption: T² versus r³ is a straight line through the origin
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <line x1="55" y1="195" x2="410" y2="195" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="55" y1="195" x2="55" y2="40" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="400" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">r^3</text>
  <text x="30" y="48" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">T^2</text>
  <line x1="55" y1="195" x2="392" y2="62" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.6"/>
  <text x="240" y="110" font-size="12.5" fill="#2f7d5a">T^2 = (4π^2/GM) r^3</text>
  <text x="230" y="228" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">a straight line: T^2 ∝ r^3; near surface T is about 84 min</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: The satellite covers one circumference $2\pi r$ in one period.
Squaring lays Kepler's third law bare — Newton deriving what Kepler observed.
The constant $4\pi^2/GM$ depends only on the central mass — same for all its satellites.
Near the surface, $T\approx 84$ min — the chapter's magic number.

segments.text: Once we have the orbital speed, the period follows immediately, and out drops Kepler's third law.
The relationship is clean: plot T squared against r cubed and you get a straight line through the origin, as the figure shows.
The satellite covers one circumference, two pi r, in one period. Divide by the orbital speed and substitute: T equals two pi root r cubed over big G M.
In words, the time for one trip is the distance around, two pi r, divided by how fast it travels.
Square it, and Kepler's third law appears: T squared equals four pi squared over big G M, times r cubed. So T squared is proportional to r cubed.
This is Newton deriving in two lines what Kepler could only observe from decades of data.
And the proportionality constant, four pi squared over big G M, depends only on the central mass — the same for every satellite of that planet.
<whisper>Near the surface, this period comes out to about eighty-four minutes — the same magic number as the tunnel oscillation and the weightless-equator day.
जैसे ही हमारे पास orbital speed है, period तुरंत निकल आता है, और Kepler का third law बाहर आ जाता है।
Relationship साफ़ है: T squared को r cubed के मुक़ाबले plot कीजिए और origin से गुज़रती एक straight line मिलती है, जैसा figure दिखाता है।
Satellite एक period में एक circumference, two pi r, तय करता है। orbital speed से divide करके substitute कीजिए: T बराबर two pi root r cubed over big G M।
शब्दों में, एक चक्कर का समय है चारों ओर की दूरी, two pi r, divided by वह कितनी तेज़ चलता है।
इसे square कीजिए, और Kepler का third law सामने आ जाता है: T squared बराबर four pi squared over big G M, into r cubed। तो T squared, r cubed के proportional है।
यह Newton का दो lines में वो derive करना है जो Kepler दशकों के data से सिर्फ़ observe कर सका।
और proportionality constant, four pi squared over big G M, सिर्फ़ central mass पर depend करता है — उस planet के हर satellite के लिए वही।
<whisper>Surface के पास, यह period लगभग चौरासी मिनट निकलता है — वही magic number जो tunnel oscillation और weightless-equator day का है।

sections.title: The energy of a satellite: K, U, and E

board_events.text: Kinetic, potential, and total energy

board_events.caption: K positive, U twice as negative, E halfway down
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <line x1="60" y1="40" x2="60" y2="235" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="52" y1="90" x2="380" y2="90" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <text x="30" y="94" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">0</text>
  <rect x="90" y="60" width="70" height="30" fill="#2f7d5a" opacity="0.5" stroke="#2f7d5a"/>
  <text x="125" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2f7d5a">K = +GMm/2r</text>
  <rect x="200" y="90" width="70" height="72" fill="#c2820a" opacity="0.45" stroke="#c2820a"/>
  <text x="235" y="178" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c2820a">E = -GMm/2r</text>
  <rect x="310" y="90" width="70" height="120" fill="#b3402f" opacity="0.4" stroke="#b3402f"/>
  <text x="345" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">U = -GMm/r</text>
  <text x="235" y="252" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">K = -E,  U = 2E,  binding energy = GMm/2r</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: So $K=-E$ and $U=2E$: total energy is negative — a bound orbit.
A higher orbit (larger $r$) has energy closer to zero — less bound, though slower.
Binding energy $=-E=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$; and $v_e=\sqrt{2}\,v_o$.

segments.text: Now the energy bookkeeping of a satellite — a JEE Main favourite, all resting on the orbital speed we just found.
Keep the energy diagram in mind: kinetic energy positive, potential energy twice as negative, and the total sitting halfway down.
The kinetic energy is one half m v o squared. Using v o squared equals big G M over r, that is big G M m over two r.
The potential energy, from the last subtopic, is minus big G M m over r.
Add them: the total energy is big G M m over two r minus big G M m over r, which is minus big G M m over two r.
Read off three things: the total energy is negative, so the orbit is bound; the kinetic energy equals the magnitude of the total, K equals minus E; and U equals two E.

One more insight: as the orbit grows, r increasing, the total energy rises toward zero. A higher orbit is a higher-energy, less tightly bound state — even though the satellite actually moves slower there.

<curious>The binding energy, the energy to send it to infinity, is minus E, big G M m over two r. And closing the loop with the last subtopic: escape velocity is root two times the orbital velocity, only about forty-one percent more.
अब एक satellite का energy का हिसाब — एक JEE Main favourite, सब उसी orbital speed पर टिका जो हमने अभी निकाली।
Energy diagram याद रखिए: kinetic energy positive, potential energy दोगुनी negative, और total बीच में नीचे बैठा।
Kinetic energy है one half m v o squared। v o squared बराबर big G M over r use करने पर, यह big G M m over two r है।
Potential energy, पिछले subtopic से, है minus big G M m over r।
इन्हें जोड़िए: total energy है big G M m over two r minus big G M m over r, यानी minus big G M m over two r।
तीन चीज़ें पढ़िए: total energy negative है, तो orbit bound है; kinetic energy total के magnitude के बराबर है, K बराबर minus E; और U बराबर two E।
एक और insight: जैसे orbit बढ़ती है, r बढ़ता है, total energy zero की तरफ उठती है। एक higher orbit एक higher-energy, कम tightly bound state है — हालाँकि satellite वहाँ असल में धीमा चलता है।

<curious>Binding energy, इसे infinity भेजने की energy, है minus E, big G M m over two r। और पिछले subtopic से loop पूरा: escape velocity, orbital velocity की root two गुना है, सिर्फ़ लगभग इकतालीस percent ज़्यादा।

sections.title: Kepler's second law, and the tools for ellipses

board_events.text: Equal areas = conserved angular momentum

board_events.caption: No torque, so L is constant; fast near, slow far
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 470 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <defs><marker id="e8" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6.5" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="#2f7d5a"/></marker></defs>
  <ellipse cx="240" cy="140" rx="180" ry="100" fill="none" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <circle cx="100" cy="140" r="15" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="100" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#22303c">Sun</text>
  <circle cx="62" cy="140" r="6" fill="#2b6ca3"/>
  <line x1="62" y1="134" x2="62" y2="88" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.6" marker-end="url(#e8)"/>
  <text x="70" y="100" font-size="10" fill="#2f7d5a">big v</text>
  <circle cx="418" cy="140" r="6" fill="#2b6ca3"/>
  <line x1="418" y1="134" x2="418" y2="112" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#e8)"/>
  <text x="388" y="112" font-size="10" fill="#2f7d5a">small v</text>
  <text x="240" y="266" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">central force, no torque → L constant → equal areas; fast near, slow far</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Gravity is a central force — it exerts no torque about the centre.
With zero torque, $L$ is constant, so equal areas are swept in equal times.
A planet speeds up near the Sun to keep $L=mvr$ fixed — areas in disguise.
These two conservation laws crack almost any two-point ellipse problem.

segments.text: The second law is really a conservation law in disguise, and it hands us the tools for elliptical orbits.
Gravity always points along the line joining satellite and planet — it is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the centre, as the figure suggests.
Because there is no torque, the satellite's angular momentum L stays constant throughout the orbit.
The area swept per unit time is L over two m. Since L and m are constant, that areal velocity is constant.
Constant areal velocity means equal areas are swept in equal times — exactly Kepler's second law.

It also explains why a planet speeds up near the Sun: with a small r, the speed v must be large to keep L equals m v r fixed. The law of areas is angular-momentum conservation wearing a geometric costume.
For an ellipse, the total energy uses the semi-major axis a: E equals minus big G M m over two a.
And at perigee and apogee, where the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, angular momentum gives the clean relation v p r p equals v a r a.
<whisper>Pair these two — energy with the semi-major axis, and angular momentum at the two turning points — and almost any two-point ellipse problem falls out without calculus.
दूसरा law असल में एक conservation law है, एक भेस में, और यह हमें elliptical orbits के tools देता है।
Gravity हमेशा satellite और planet को जोड़ने वाली line के साथ point करती है — यह एक central force है, तो यह centre के बारे में कोई torque नहीं लगाती, जैसा figure सुझाता है।
चूँकि कोई torque नहीं, satellite का angular momentum L पूरी orbit में constant रहता है।
Per unit time sweep किया area है L over two m। चूँकि L और m constant हैं, वो areal velocity constant है।
Constant areal velocity का मतलब बराबर समय में बराबर areas sweep होते हैं — बिलकुल Kepler का second law।

यह यह भी समझाता है कि planet Sun के पास तेज़ क्यों होता है: छोटे r के साथ, speed v को बड़ा होना चाहिए ताकि L बराबर m v r fixed रहे। law of areas, angular-momentum conservation है एक geometric पोशाक में।
एक ellipse के लिए, total energy semi-major axis a use करती है: E बराबर minus big G M m over two a।
और perigee और apogee पर, जहाँ velocity radius के perpendicular है, angular momentum देता है साफ़ relation v p r p बराबर v a r a।
<whisper>इन दोनों को जोड़िए — energy के साथ semi-major axis, और दोनों turning points पर angular momentum — और लगभग कोई भी two-point ellipse problem बिना calculus के निकल आता है।

sections.title: Worked example: a low-Earth-orbit satellite (CBSE)

board_events.text: Orbital speed and period at 600 km

board_events.caption: Orbital radius r = R + h
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="140" cy="120" r="82" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <circle cx="140" cy="120" r="70" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="140" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">Earth</text>
  <circle cx="222" cy="120" r="7" fill="#b3402f"/>
  <text x="234" y="112" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">600 km</text>
  <text x="330" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2b6ca3">r = R + h = 7.0×10^6 m</text>
  <text x="330" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2f7d5a">v_o ≈ 7.6 km/s</text>
  <text x="330" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">T ≈ 97 min</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Height 600 km, so $r=R+h=7.0\times10^6$ m.
That is about 97 minutes for one orbit.
A low-Earth satellite circles roughly every hour and a half — like the ISS.

segments.text: A clean board example. A satellite orbits at a height of six hundred kilometres above the surface. Find its orbital speed and its period.
First get the orbital radius. The height is six hundred kilometres, so r equals R plus h, which is seven times ten to the six metres.
Remember to add the Earth's radius to the height — the orbit radius is measured from the centre, not the surface.
Now the speed. v o is the square root of big G M over r: put in the constants, the Earth's mass, and that radius.
Inside the root is five point seven two times ten to the seven, so v o is about seven point six times ten to the three metres per second — seven point six kilometres per second.

For the period, divide the circumference two pi r by the speed: two pi times seven times ten to the six, over seven point six times ten to the three, about five point eight times ten to the three seconds.
That is roughly ninety-seven minutes for one full orbit.
<curious>So a low-Earth satellite circles the planet about every hour and a half — consistent with the Space Station, which loops the Earth roughly sixteen times a day.
एक साफ़ board example। एक satellite surface से छह सौ kilometres की height पर orbit करता है। इसकी orbital speed और period निकालिए।
पहले orbital radius लीजिए। height छह सौ kilometres है, तो r बराबर R plus h, यानी seven into ten to the six metres।
याद रखिए height में Earth का radius जोड़ना है — orbit radius centre से नापा जाता है, surface से नहीं।
अब speed। v o है square root of big G M over r: constants, Earth का mass, और वो radius रखिए।
Root के अंदर है five point seven two into ten to the seven, तो v o लगभग seven point six into ten to the three metres per second है — seven point six kilometres per second।
Period के लिए, circumference two pi r को speed से divide कीजिए: two pi into seven into ten to the six, over seven point six into ten to the three, लगभग five point eight into ten to the three seconds।
यह एक पूरी orbit के लिए क़रीब सत्तानवे मिनट है।
<curious>तो एक low-Earth satellite planet के चारों ओर लगभग हर डेढ़ घंटे में घूमता है — Space Station के अनुरूप, जो Earth के लगभग सोलह चक्कर रोज़ लगाता है।

sections.title: Worked example: scaling the period with radius (NEET)

board_events.text: Radius up 4×: what happens to the period?

board_events.caption: T ∝ r^(3/2): quadruple r multiplies T by 8

<svg viewBox="0 0 440 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="150" cy="120" r="18" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <circle cx="150" cy="120" r="45" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <circle cx="150" cy="120" r="105" fill="none" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="150" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#2b6ca3">r (T = 6 h)</text>
  <text x="150" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">4r</text>
  <text x="330" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">T ∝ r^(3/2)</text>
  <text x="330" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">(4)^(3/2) = 8</text>
  <text x="330" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#b3402f">T: 6 h → 48 h</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A satellite's period is 6 hours; its radius is increased to 4× the original.
Trap: $4\times6=24$ h treats $T\propto r$ — wrong; the exponent is 3/2.
Cube the radius factor, then square-root it: $4^3=64$, $\sqrt{64}=8$.

segments.text: A quick NEET scaling problem, done entirely with Kepler's third law. A satellite's period is six hours. Its orbital radius is increased to four times the original. What is the new period?
Reason as a ratio. Since T squared is proportional to r cubed, the period is proportional to r to the three halves, as the figure notes.
So we do not recompute anything — we just scale the period by the radius factor raised to the right power.
From T squared proportional to r cubed, take the square root: T is proportional to r to the three halves.
So the ratio of periods is four to the three halves. That is the radius factor cubed, then square-rooted.
Four cubed is sixty-four, and the square root of sixty-four is eight. So the new period is eight times six, which is forty-eight hours.
The tempting wrong answer is four times six, twenty-four hours, which treats T as proportional to r. Another is applying the wrong power.
<whisper>Respect the three-halves exponent: cube the radius factor, then take the square root. Four cubed is sixty-four, root sixty-four is eight — a five-second mental calculation.
एक तेज़ NEET scaling problem, पूरी तरह Kepler के third law से। एक satellite का period छह घंटे है। इसका orbital radius original के चार गुना बढ़ा दिया जाता है। नया period क्या है?
एक ratio की तरह reason कीजिए। चूँकि T squared, r cubed के proportional है, period, r to the three halves के proportional है, जैसा figure बताता है।
तो हम कुछ भी दोबारा compute नहीं करते — हम बस period को radius factor की सही power से scale करते हैं।
T squared proportional to r cubed से, square root लीजिए: T, r to the three halves के proportional है।
तो periods का ratio है four to the three halves। यानी radius factor cubed, फिर square-rooted।
Four cubed है चौंसठ, और चौंसठ का square root है eight। तो नया period है eight into six, यानी अड़तालीस घंटे।
लुभावना ग़लत जवाब है four into six, चौबीस घंटे, जो T को r के proportional मानता है। एक और है ग़लत power लगाना।
<whisper>Three-halves exponent की इज़्ज़त कीजिए: radius factor को cube कीजिए, फिर square root लीजिए। four cubed है चौंसठ, root चौंसठ है eight — एक पाँच-second का mental calculation।

sections.title: Worked example: the geostationary altitude (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Where must a 24-hour satellite orbit?

board_events.caption: Period fixed at 24 h sets a single radius
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="150" cy="140" r="118" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
  <circle cx="150" cy="140" r="52" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="150" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">Earth</text>
  <circle cx="268" cy="140" r="7" fill="#c2820a"/>
  <text x="268" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#c2820a">sat</text>
  <text x="360" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">T = 24 h</text>
  <text x="360" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2b6ca3">r = 4.2×10^7 m</text>
  <text x="360" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2f7d5a">h ≈ 36000 km ≈ 6R</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A geostationary satellite matches the Earth's rotation: $T=24$ h $=86400$ s.
Compute inside: $GM=4.0\times10^{14}$, $T^2=7.47\times10^9$.
Every TV and weather satellite over the equator sits at this one altitude (≈6R).

segments.text: Now derive the special height every communications satellite uses. Find the altitude at which a geostationary satellite must orbit.
The single condition, shown in the figure, is that its period must equal the Earth's rotation period, twenty-four hours, or eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds.
That one requirement fixes everything, because for a given central mass, the period pins the radius.
From T squared equals four pi squared r cubed over big G M, solve for r: r is big G M times T squared, over four pi squared, all to the one third.
Compute the pieces: big G M is four times ten to the fourteen, and T squared is seven point four seven times ten to the nine.
Multiply the top and divide by four pi squared, about thirty-nine point five: r cubed is seven point five six times ten to the twenty-two cubic metres.
Take the cube root: r is about four point two times ten to the seven metres. Subtract the Earth's radius to get the height, about thirty-six thousand kilometres.
<excited>So every television and weather satellite parked over the equator sits at this single special altitude, roughly six Earth-radii up — the only height where the period matches the day.
अब वो ख़ास height derive कीजिए जो हर communications satellite use करता है। वो altitude निकालिए जहाँ एक geostationary satellite को orbit करना चाहिए।
एकमात्र condition, जो figure में दिखाई है, यह है कि इसका period Earth के rotation period के बराबर होना चाहिए, चौबीस घंटे, यानी छियासी हज़ार चार सौ seconds।
वो एक requirement सब कुछ तय कर देती है, क्योंकि एक दिए central mass के लिए, period, radius को pin कर देता है।
T squared बराबर four pi squared r cubed over big G M से, r के लिए हल कीजिए: r है big G M into T squared, over four pi squared, पूरा to the one third।
टुकड़े compute कीजिए: big G M है four into ten to the fourteen, और T squared है seven point four seven into ten to the nine।
ऊपर को multiply करके four pi squared, लगभग उनतालीस point five से divide कीजिए: r cubed है seven point five six into ten to the twenty-two cubic metres।
Cube root लीजिए: r लगभग four point two into ten to the seven metres है। Earth का radius घटाकर height पाइए, लगभग छत्तीस हज़ार kilometres।
<excited>तो equator के ऊपर खड़ा हर television और weather satellite इसी एक ख़ास altitude पर बैठता है, क़रीब छह Earth-radii ऊपर — एकमात्र height जहाँ period दिन से मेल खाता है।

board_events.text: Boost the speed and find the far point

board_events.caption: Burn point becomes perigee; find the apogee

  <text x="150" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#22303c">planet</text>
  <circle cx="102" cy="140" r="6" fill="#b3402f"/>
  <text x="88" y="128" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">perigee r_0</text>
  <line x1="102" y1="128" x2="102" y2="86" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#e12)"/>
  <text x="108" y="98" font-size="10" fill="#2f7d5a">burn</text>
  <circle cx="435" cy="140" r="6" fill="#b3402f"/>
  <text x="420" y="128" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">apogee 3r_0</text>
  <text x="245" y="266" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">boost to √(3/2) v_0 → ellipse with apogee r_a = 3r_0</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Circular $v_0=\sqrt{GM/r_0}$; boost to $v=\sqrt{3/2}\,v_0$ tangentially.
Since $v_0<v<\sqrt{2}\,v_0=v_e$, the orbit stays bound — an ellipse.
A modest ~22% speed boost triples the far-point distance — orbits are touchy.

segments.text: A signature JEE Advanced problem using two conservation laws together. A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius r naught. A brief engine burn suddenly increases its speed to root three over two times the circular speed, still tangential. Find the maximum distance it reaches.
The burn point, at radius r naught, becomes the perigee — the closest approach — and we want the apogee, the far point, as the figure shows.
The circular speed is v naught, root big G M over r naught. The boosted speed is root three over two times that.
Since the new speed is between v naught and root two v naught, which is the escape speed, the satellite stays bound — it moves onto an ellipse.
Now two conservation laws. Angular momentum, with velocity perpendicular to the radius at both ends, gives m v r naught equals m v a r a, so v a is v r naught over r a.
Energy conservation: one half v squared minus big G M over r naught equals one half v a squared minus big G M over r a.
Substitute the boosted speed and v a, simplify, and you reach a quadratic that factors as r a minus r naught, times r a minus three r naught.
The roots are r a equals r naught, the perigee we started from, and r a equals three r naught, the apogee. So the maximum distance is three r naught.
<excited>A modest boost of root one point five, only about twenty-two percent more speed, triples the far-point distance. That steep sensitivity is why orbital insertions demand such precision.

एक signature JEE Advanced problem, दो conservation laws साथ use करते हुए। एक satellite radius r naught की circular orbit में है। एक छोटा engine burn अचानक इसकी speed को circular speed की root three over two गुना बढ़ा देता है, अब भी tangential। यह जो अधिकतम distance पहुँचता है, निकालिए।
Burn point, radius r naught पर, perigee बन जाता है — सबसे क़रीबी approach — और हमें apogee चाहिए, दूर वाला point, जैसा figure दिखाता है।
Circular speed है v naught, root big G M over r naught। boosted speed उसकी root three over two गुना है।
चूँकि नई speed, v naught और root two v naught, यानी escape speed, के बीच है, satellite bound रहता है — यह एक ellipse पर चला जाता है।
अब दो conservation laws। angular momentum, दोनों सिरों पर velocity radius के perpendicular के साथ, देता है m v r naught बराबर m v a r a, तो v a है v r naught over r a।
Energy conservation: one half v squared minus big G M over r naught बराबर one half v a squared minus big G M over r a।
Boosted speed और v a substitute करके simplify कीजिए, और आप एक quadratic तक पहुँचते हैं जो factor होता है r a minus r naught, into r a minus three r naught।
Roots हैं r a बराबर r naught, वो perigee जहाँ से शुरू किया, और r a बराबर three r naught, apogee। तो अधिकतम distance है three r naught।

<excited>root one point five का एक मामूली boost, सिर्फ़ लगभग बाईस percent ज़्यादा speed, दूर वाले point की distance तिगुनी कर देता है। यही steep sensitivity वजह है कि orbital insertions इतनी precision माँगते हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for satellites

board_events.text: Satellites: the traps and the shortcuts
1. Kepler III is $T\propto r^{3/2}$, not $T\propto r$: quadruple $r$ gives ×8 period.
2. 'Weightless' means shared free fall, not absent gravity — state it that way.
3. Satellite energy $E=-GMm/2r$ is negative and half of $|U|$ — keep the sign.
4. $v_e=\sqrt{2}\,v_o$: only ~41% separates orbiting from escaping.
For ellipses, let conservation do the work: $v_p r_p=v_a r_a$ plus energy.
Magic numbers: near-surface $v_o\approx 7.9$ km/s, $T\approx 84$ min; $v_e\approx 11.2$ km/s.
Geostationary: $T=24$ h, $h\approx 36000$ km, $v_o\approx 3.1$ km/s.

segments.text: Let us close Part five with the satellite traps and the shortcuts that turn many questions into instant recognition.

Trap one: scaling the period linearly. Kepler's third law is T proportional to r to the three halves, not to r. Quadrupling the radius multiplies the period by eight, not four. Cube the radius factor, then take the square root.
Trap two: thinking weightless means no gravity. Orbiting astronauts are in free fall with nearly full gravity acting. State it as shared free fall in exams — examiners test this exact misconception.

Trap three: mishandling satellite energy. The total energy is minus big G M m over two r — negative, and half the magnitude of the potential energy. Writing minus big G M m over r, which is U not E, or dropping the sign, is a costly slip.
Trap four: confusing orbital and escape velocity. Escape velocity is root two times orbital velocity, only about forty-one percent more. Mixing them reverses whether an orbit is bound.
The main shortcut: for elliptical orbits, let conservation laws do the work. At perigee and apogee, angular momentum gives v p r p equals v a r a; pair it with energy conservation.
And memorise the magic numbers: a near-surface orbit has speed about seven point nine kilometres per second and period about eighty-four minutes; escape speed is about eleven point two.

<whisper>For geostationary, remember the trio: period twenty-four hours, height about thirty-six thousand kilometres, orbital speed about three point one kilometres per second. Those turn many questions into instant recognition.
Part five को satellite के traps और उन shortcuts के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो कई सवालों को तुरंत पहचान में बदल देते हैं।

Trap one: period को linearly scale करना। Kepler का third law है T proportional to r to the three halves, r के नहीं। radius चार गुना करने पर period आठ गुना होता है, चार नहीं। radius factor को cube कीजिए, फिर square root लीजिए।

Trap two: यह सोचना कि weightless का मतलब no gravity है। orbit करते astronauts free fall में हैं, लगभग पूरी gravity act करते हुए। exams में इसे shared free fall कहिए — examiners यही misconception test करते हैं।

Trap three: satellite energy को ग़लत संभालना। total energy है minus big G M m over two r — negative, और potential energy के magnitude का आधा। minus big G M m over r लिखना, जो U है E नहीं, या sign गिराना, एक महँगी चूक है।

Trap four: orbital और escape velocity को confuse करना। escape velocity, orbital velocity की root two गुना है, सिर्फ़ लगभग इकतालीस percent ज़्यादा। इन्हें mix करना उलट देता है कि orbit bound है या नहीं।
मुख्य shortcut: elliptical orbits के लिए, conservation laws को काम करने दीजिए। perigee और apogee पर, angular momentum देता है v p r p बराबर v a r a; इसे energy conservation के साथ जोड़िए।
और magic numbers याद रखिए: एक near-surface orbit की speed लगभग seven point nine kilometres per second और period लगभग चौरासी मिनट है; escape speed लगभग eleven point two है।

<whisper>Geostationary के लिए, तिकड़ी याद रखिए: period चौबीस घंटे, height लगभग छत्तीस हज़ार kilometres, orbital speed लगभग three point one kilometres per second। ये कई सवालों को तुरंत पहचान में बदल देते हैं।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Why orbits give only GM, and how Cavendish weighed G

board_events.text: Where does the number G come from?
Every orbit gives only the PRODUCT $GM$ — $G$ and $M$ are always glued together.

board_events.caption: A torsion balance turns a tiny pull into a readable twist

board_events.text: To prise $G$ loose, measure the pull between two masses you can weigh in a lab.
Gravity is so weak the pull between two lead balls is like a grain of sand's weight.
Cavendish's genius: make the tiny force reveal itself as a twist, not a push.
A mirror on the fibre throws a light beam across the room — an optical lever.
He built an amplifier for the weakest force in nature.

segments.text: We have used big G throughout the chapter as if it fell from the sky. But where does its value actually come from?
Here is the catch. You cannot read big G off the motion of planets, because every orbit gives you only the product big G M. Look back at orbital velocity — big G and M are always glued together.
To prise big G loose, you must measure the gravitational force between two masses you can weigh in a laboratory. The figure shows how Cavendish did it.
And therein lies the difficulty: gravity is so absurdly weak that the attraction between two lead balls on a table is comparable to the weight of a single grain of sand.
Measuring that is like detecting a whisper in a hurricane — the pull is buried under air currents, vibrations, and the whole Earth's pull.

Cavendish's stroke of genius, in seventeen ninety-eight, was to make the tiny force reveal itself not as a push but as a twist. He hung a light dumbbell from a fine fibre and brought large masses near.
The minuscule attraction twisted the fibre by a hair's breadth — but a mirror on the fibre threw a beam of light across the room, turning that twist into a large, readable swing on a distant scale.
<excited>He had built an amplifier for the weakest force in nature — and measuring big G then let him do something breathtaking: weigh the Earth.
हमने पूरे chapter में big G ऐसे use किया जैसे यह आसमान से टपका हो। पर इसकी value असल में कहाँ से आती है?
यहाँ पेच है। आप big G को planets की motion से पढ़ नहीं सकते, क्योंकि हर orbit आपको सिर्फ़ product big G M देती है। orbital velocity पर वापस देखिए — big G और M हमेशा एक साथ चिपके होते हैं।
big G को अलग निकालने के लिए, आपको दो ऐसे masses के बीच gravitational force नापना होगा जिन्हें आप lab में तौल सकें। figure दिखाता है कि Cavendish ने यह कैसे किया।
और यहीं मुश्किल है: gravity इतनी बेहद weak है कि एक मेज़ पर दो lead balls के बीच का attraction, रेत के एक दाने के weight जितना है।
इसे नापना एक तूफ़ान में फुसफुसाहट पकड़ने जैसा है — pull हवा की धाराओं, कंपन, और पूरी Earth के pull के नीचे दबा है।
Cavendish का genius का कदम, सत्रह सौ अठानवे में, यह था कि tiny force को push नहीं बल्कि एक twist के रूप में सामने लाया जाए। उन्होंने एक हल्का dumbbell एक बारीक fibre से लटकाया और बड़े masses पास लाए।
उस बेहद छोटे attraction ने fibre को बाल भर घुमाया — पर fibre पर एक mirror ने कमरे भर में light का एक beam फेंका, उस twist को एक दूर scale पर एक बड़े, पढ़ने योग्य swing में बदलते हुए।
<excited>उन्होंने प्रकृति के सबसे weak force का एक amplifier बना लिया था — और फिर big G नापने से वे कुछ हैरतअंगेज़ कर सके: Earth को तौलना।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Weighing the Earth once G is known

board_events.text: From surface gravity to the Earth's mass

board_events.caption: g and R hand you the Earth's mass and density
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="140" cy="120" r="88" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="140" cy="120" r="38" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="140" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">dense core</text>
  <text x="330" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#2b6ca3">M = gR^2 / G</text>
  <text x="330" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2f7d5a">≈ 6×10^24 kg</text>
  <text x="330" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">ρ ≈ 5.5× water</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Once $G$ is known, the Earth's own surface gravity gives its mass.
We never had to leave the ground — just $g$, $R$, and a lab value of $G$.
Cavendish's real goal was the density — about 5.5 times water.
That revealed the deep interior is far denser than the crust — a hint of the iron core.

segments.text: Once big G is measured, the Earth's own surface gravity hands us its mass — no space mission required.
The figure captures it. Knowing g and R, and now big G, everything about the Earth's bulk follows.
Start from g equals big G M over R squared. Solve for the mass.
That gives M equals g R squared over big G. Put in nine point eight and the Earth's radius, and out comes about six times ten to the twenty-four kilograms.
Pause on how remarkable that is: we weighed the entire planet without ever leaving the ground — just the acceleration of a falling apple, the Earth's radius, and a lab value of big G.
The mean density follows too. Using mass equals four thirds pi R cubed rho, the density is three g over four pi big G R.
This was actually Cavendish's real goal. He reported the Earth's density, about five and a half times that of water.
<curious>And that number was a revelation: since surface rock is only about half as dense, the deep interior must be far denser — the very first hint of the Earth's iron core.
जैसे ही big G नापी जाती है, Earth का अपना surface gravity हमें इसका mass दे देता है — कोई space mission ज़रूरी नहीं।
Figure इसे पकड़ता है। g और R जानकर, और अब big G, Earth के पूरे bulk के बारे में सब कुछ निकल आता है।
g बराबर big G M over R squared से शुरू कीजिए। mass के लिए हल कीजिए।
इससे मिलता है M बराबर g R squared over big G। nine point eight और Earth का radius रखिए, और निकलता है लगभग six into ten to the twenty-four kilograms।
यह कितना उल्लेखनीय है इस पर रुकिए: हमने पूरे planet को तौला बिना कभी ज़मीन छोड़े — बस एक गिरते सेब का acceleration, Earth का radius, और big G की एक lab value।
Mean density भी निकल आती है। mass बराबर four thirds pi R cubed rho use करते हुए, density है three g over four pi big G R।
यह असल में Cavendish का असली लक्ष्य था। उन्होंने Earth की density बताई, लगभग पानी की साढ़े पाँच गुना।
<curious>और वो number एक ख़ुलासा था: चूँकि surface rock सिर्फ़ लगभग आधी घनी है, गहरा interior कहीं ज़्यादा घना होना चाहिए — Earth के iron core का पहला संकेत।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: When both masses move: binaries and reduced mass

board_events.text: Newton's third law strikes back

board_events.caption: Neither is the centre — both orbit the balance point
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="150" cy="130" r="80" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <circle cx="270" cy="130" r="55" fill="none" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="222" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#22303c">×</text>
  <text x="222" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">C</text>
  <circle cx="70" cy="130" r="12" fill="#2b6ca3"/>
  <text x="70" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">m_1</text>
  <circle cx="325" cy="130" r="18" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="325" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">m_2</text>
  <text x="220" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">both orbit the common centre of mass with the same period</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: We treated one body as fixed and the other as orbiting — a convenient fiction.
But the satellite pulls the Earth just as hard (Newton's third law).
When masses are comparable — two stars, a planet and a heavy moon — both bodies move.
Each orbits their common centre of mass; two stars in mutual orbit is a binary.
The reduced mass collapses this two-body dance to one equivalent body.
Then every earlier orbit formula snaps back into use.

segments.text: The second big idea in this Part fixes an approximation we have quietly leaned on all chapter.
The figure shows the fix. We always treated one body as a fixed centre and the other as a small thing orbiting it — Earth fixed, satellite circling.
That was a convenient fiction. In reality, both bodies respond to the pull between them.
Newton's third law insists the satellite pulls the Earth just as hard as the Earth pulls the satellite.
When the two masses are comparable — two stars, or a planet and a heavy moon — you can no longer pretend one is fixed. Both bodies genuinely move.
Each orbits their common balance point, the centre of mass. Two stars locked in mutual orbit, a binary system, is the cleanest example — neither is the centre, they waltz around a point between them.
Remarkably, this two-body dance can be reduced to a single equivalent one-body problem, using a clever quantity called the reduced mass.
<curious>And once you do that, all our earlier single-body orbit formulas snap right back into use — the hard problem becomes the easy one in disguise.
इस Part का दूसरा बड़ा idea एक approximation को ठीक करता है जिस पर हम पूरे chapter चुपचाप टिके रहे।
Figure fix दिखाता है। हमने हमेशा एक body को एक fixed centre और दूसरी को उसके चारों ओर घूमती एक छोटी चीज़ माना — Earth fixed, satellite circling।
वो एक सुविधाजनक कल्पना थी। असल में, दोनों bodies उनके बीच के pull को respond करती हैं।
Newton का third law ज़ोर देता है कि satellite, Earth को उतनी ही ज़ोर से खींचता है जितना Earth satellite को।
जब दोनों masses comparable हों — दो stars, या एक planet और एक भारी moon — आप अब एक को fixed नहीं मान सकते। दोनों bodies सचमुच चलती हैं।

हर एक अपने common balance point, centre of mass, के चारों ओर orbit करती है। mutual orbit में बँधे दो stars, एक binary system, सबसे साफ़ उदाहरण है — कोई भी centre नहीं है, वे बीच के एक point के चारों ओर नाचते हैं।
उल्लेखनीय है, इस two-body नृत्य को एक single equivalent one-body problem में घटाया जा सकता है, एक चतुर quantity की मदद से जिसे reduced mass कहते हैं।
<curious>और ऐसा करते ही, हमारे सारे पहले वाले single-body orbit formulas वापस काम में आ जाते हैं — मुश्किल problem एक भेस में आसान बन जाती है।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Tides: the difference in pull across a body

board_events.text: Why the oceans bulge on both sides

board_events.caption: Near water pulled more, far water less — two bulges
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 470 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <ellipse cx="170" cy="120" rx="92" ry="66" fill="#2b6ca3" opacity="0.25" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <circle cx="170" cy="120" r="58" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.8"/>
  <text x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">Earth</text>
  <circle cx="410" cy="120" r="22" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="410" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">Moon</text>
  <text x="170" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c">near water pulled more, far water less → two bulges, two high tides a day</text>
  <text x="170" y="30" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">tides ∝ 1/r^3, so the near Moon beats the Sun</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Gravity weakens with distance, so the near side is pulled more than the far side.
This difference across a body is a tidal force — it stretches the body toward its companion.
The oceans bulge toward AND away from the Moon — so most coasts see two high tides a day.
The Sun pulls the Earth far harder, yet the Moon dominates the tides.
Tides depend on how fast the pull CHANGES ($\propto 1/r^3$), not the pull itself ($\propto 1/r^2$).
Pushed far enough, tidal forces tear a moon apart inside the Roche limit — the origin of rings.

segments.text: One more two-body consequence is worth knowing, and it explains something you can see at any coast: the tides.
Because gravity weakens with distance, an extended body feels a stronger pull on its near side than on its far side, as the figure shows.
That difference in pull, from one side of a body to the other, is what matters — not the pull itself.
This difference across a body is called a tidal force, and it stretches the body along the line to its companion.

So the Earth's oceans bulge out both toward the Moon and away from it — the near water is pulled toward the Moon more than the solid Earth, the far water less. That is why most coasts see roughly two high tides a day.
Now a puzzle. The Sun pulls the Earth far harder than the Moon does — yet the Moon dominates the tides. How?

Because tides depend on how rapidly the pull changes across the Earth, which falls off as one over r cubed, not on the pull itself, which falls off as one over r squared. The nearby Moon wins that steeper comparison.
<excited>Pushed to an extreme, tidal forces can tear a moon apart if it strays inside a critical distance called the Roche limit — and that is the very origin of planetary rings.
एक और two-body नतीजा जानने लायक़ है, और यह कुछ समझाता है जो आप किसी भी तट पर देख सकते हैं: tides।
चूँकि gravity distance के साथ weak होती है, एक extended body अपने near side पर far side से ज़्यादा strong pull महसूस करती है, जैसा figure दिखाता है।
Pull में वो फ़र्क़, body के एक side से दूसरे तक, ही मायने रखता है — pull ख़ुद नहीं।
Body के आर-पार यह फ़र्क़ tidal force कहलाता है, और यह body को उसके companion की तरफ की line के साथ खींचता है।
तो Earth के oceans, Moon की तरफ और उससे दूर, दोनों तरफ उभरते हैं — near water solid Earth से ज़्यादा Moon की तरफ खिंचता है, far water कम। इसीलिए ज़्यादातर तट रोज़ लगभग दो high tides देखते हैं।
अब एक पहेली। Sun, Earth को Moon से कहीं ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींचता है — फिर भी Moon tides पर हावी है। कैसे?

क्योंकि tides इस पर depend करती हैं कि Earth के आर-पार pull कितनी तेज़ी से बदलता है, जो one over r cubed के हिसाब से गिरता है, न कि pull पर ख़ुद, जो one over r squared के हिसाब से। पास वाला Moon वो steeper comparison जीतता है।
<excited>Extreme तक धकेलने पर, tidal forces एक moon को फाड़ सकती हैं अगर वो एक critical distance, जिसे Roche limit कहते हैं, के अंदर भटक जाए — और यही planetary rings का असली मूल है।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: The Cavendish relation for G

board_events.text: Balancing gravitational torque against the fibre

board_events.caption: At equilibrium, gravitational torque = fibre torque
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <defs>
    <marker id="f5g" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 Z" fill="#2f7d5a"/></marker>
    <marker id="f5r" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 Z" fill="#b3402f"/></marker>
  </defs>
  <line x1="90" y1="100" x2="290" y2="100" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="190" cy="100" r="4" fill="#22303c"/>
  <text x="190" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">fibre</text>
  <line x1="290" y1="100" x2="290" y2="52" stroke="#2f7d5a" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#f5g)"/>
  <text x="300" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#2f7d5a">F</text>
  <text x="230" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">L</text>
  <path d="M190,130 A22 22 0 0 1 210 138" fill="none" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#f5r)"/>
  <text x="214" y="150" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">θ</text>
  <text x="235" y="196" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c">F×L = κθ  →  G = κθd^2 / (MmL)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Each large mass pulls a small one with $F=GMm/d^2$; the couple's torque is $F\times L$.
$\theta$ is read from the light-spot deflection; $\kappa$ from the torsional period.
Cavendish reached within about 1% of the modern value — in 1798.

segments.text: Let us write the working relation Cavendish used to extract big G from his balance.
The rod settles where two torques balance, as the figure shows: the gravitational couple twisting it, and the fibre resisting.

Each large sphere pulls its nearby small sphere with a force big G M m over d squared. Because the two act on opposite ends, they form a couple, whose torque about the fibre is that force times the rod length L.

At equilibrium, the gravitational torque equals the fibre's restoring torque: big G M m over d squared, times L, equals kappa theta, where kappa is the fibre's torsion constant and theta the twist angle.
Solve for the unknown, big G, and you get kappa theta d squared, over M m L.
The twist theta is read from the deflection of the reflected light-spot on a far scale — the optical lever that magnifies the tiny angle enormously.
And the torsion constant kappa is found separately, by timing the free torsional oscillations of the rod: their period is two pi root I over kappa, with I the moment of inertia.
<excited>With this, Cavendish reached within about one percent of the modern value of big G — an extraordinary feat for seventeen ninety-eight.
आइए वो working relation लिखें जो Cavendish ने अपने balance से big G निकालने के लिए use किया।
Rod वहाँ ठहरती है जहाँ दो torques balance होते हैं, जैसा figure दिखाता है: gravitational couple इसे घुमाता, और fibre विरोध करता।

हर बड़ा sphere अपने पास वाले छोटे sphere को force big G M m over d squared से खींचता है। चूँकि दोनों opposite सिरों पर act करते हैं, वे एक couple बनाते हैं, जिसका fibre के बारे में torque है वो force into rod length L।
Equilibrium पर, gravitational torque, fibre के restoring torque के बराबर है: big G M m over d squared, into L, बराबर kappa theta, जहाँ kappa fibre का torsion constant और theta twist angle है।
अनजान, big G, के लिए हल कीजिए, और मिलता है kappa theta d squared, over M m L।
Twist theta एक दूर scale पर परावर्तित light-spot के deflection से पढ़ा जाता है — वो optical lever जो tiny angle को ज़बरदस्त बड़ा कर देता है।
और torsion constant kappa अलग से निकाला जाता है, rod के free torsional oscillations को time करके: उनका period है two pi root I over kappa, I moment of inertia के साथ।
<excited>इससे, Cavendish big G की modern value के लगभग एक percent के भीतर पहुँचे — सत्रह सौ अठानवे के लिए एक असाधारण कारनामा।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Mass and mean density of the Earth

board_events.text: Two one-line results from g

board_events.caption: The mean density comes straight from g, R, and G
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="120" cy="100" r="74" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="120" cy="100" r="30" fill="#c2820a" opacity="0.7"/>
  <text x="320" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#2b6ca3">ρ = 3g / (4πGR)</text>
  <text x="320" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2f7d5a">≈ 5.5×10^3 kg/m^3</text>
  <text x="320" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#22303c">the core must be far denser</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: From $g=GM/R^2$, rearrange for the mass. Put in $g=9.8$, $R=6.4\times10^6$ m.
About 5.5× water — the interior is far denser than the crust.

segments.text: Here are the two clean results, stated as formulas, that the Cavendish value unlocks.
As the figure notes, once big G is known, g and R alone give both the Earth's mass and its mean density.
The mass is g R squared over big G — just the surface-gravity relation, rearranged.
Substitute nine point eight for g and six point four times ten to the six metres for R, with the lab value of big G.
The mass comes out to about six times ten to the twenty-four kilograms.
For the density, divide the mass by the volume, four thirds pi R cubed. The R cubed partly cancels, leaving three g over four pi big G R.
Numerically, that is about five point five times ten to the three kilograms per cubic metre.
<curious>That is roughly five and a half times the density of water — and since surface rock is much lighter, the interior must be far denser, pointing to the iron core.
यहाँ वो दो साफ़ results हैं, formulas के रूप में, जो Cavendish की value खोल देती है।
जैसा figure बताता है, जैसे ही big G ज्ञात है, g और R अकेले Earth का mass और उसकी mean density दोनों दे देते हैं।
Mass है g R squared over big G — बस surface-gravity relation, rearrange किया।
g के लिए nine point eight और R के लिए six point four into ten to the six metres रखिए, big G की lab value के साथ।
Mass निकलता है लगभग six into ten to the twenty-four kilograms।
Density के लिए, mass को volume, four thirds pi R cubed, से divide कीजिए। R cubed आंशिक रूप से cancel होता है, बचता है three g over four pi big G R।
Numerically, यह लगभग five point five into ten to the three kilograms per cubic metre है।
<curious>यह पानी की density की लगभग साढ़े पाँच गुना है — और चूँकि surface rock बहुत हल्की है, interior कहीं ज़्यादा घना होना चाहिए, iron core की ओर इशारा करते हुए।

sections.title: The two-body problem and reduced mass

board_events.text: Both bodies orbit the centre of mass

board_events.caption: The heavier star traces the smaller circle

  <text x="300" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">2m</text>
  <text x="237" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#b3402f">×</text>
  <text x="237" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">C</text>
  <line x1="110" y1="140" x2="237" y2="140" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <text x="173" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#2b6ca3">r_1</text>
  <line x1="237" y1="140" x2="300" y2="140" stroke="#c2820a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <text x="268" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#c2820a">r_2</text>
  <text x="220" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303c">m r_1 = 2m r_2  →  heavier star, smaller circle (r ∝ 1/m)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: The centre of mass divides the separation inversely to the masses.
Kepler's third law, but with the SUM of the masses — how binary stars are weighed.
When $m_2\gg m_1$, $\mu\to m_1$ — recovering the fixed-centre approximation.

segments.text: Now the formulas for two comparable masses orbiting their common centre of mass.
The figure shows the key geometry. The centre of mass sits closer to the heavier star, so the heavier star traces the smaller circle.
Quantitatively, r one, the lighter star's orbit radius, is m two r over the total mass, and in general m one r one equals m two r two.
In words: the centre of mass divides the separation inversely to the masses. Heavier means closer in, on a tighter circle.
Applying gravity as the centripetal force for one body and cancelling, the angular velocity satisfies omega squared equals big G times the total mass, over r cubed.

This is Kepler's third law again, but with the sum of the two masses in place of a single central mass — which is exactly how astronomers weigh binary stars: measure T and r, and read off m one plus m two.
Define the reduced mass, mu equals m one m two over the total mass. It collapses the two-body problem to a single body of mass mu orbiting a fixed centre.
So the period is two pi root r cubed over big G times the total mass, and the bound binary's total energy is minus big G m one m two over two r.

<curious>And the beautiful limit: when one mass hugely exceeds the other, the reduced mass tends to the smaller mass, and the heavier body becomes the fixed centre — recovering exactly the approximation we made for satellites.
अब दो comparable masses के formulas जो अपने common centre of mass के चारों ओर orbit करते हैं।
Figure key geometry दिखाता है। centre of mass भारी star के क़रीब बैठता है, तो भारी star छोटा circle बनाता है।
मात्रात्मक रूप से, r one, हल्के star का orbit radius, है m two r over total mass, और आम तौर पर m one r one बराबर m two r two।
शब्दों में: centre of mass, separation को masses के inversely बाँटता है। भारी मतलब ज़्यादा अंदर, एक tighter circle पर।
एक body के लिए gravity को centripetal force के तौर पर लगाकर और cancel करके, angular velocity satisfy करती है omega squared बराबर big G into total mass, over r cubed।
यह फिर Kepler का third law है, पर एक single central mass की जगह दोनों masses के sum के साथ — यही तरीक़ा है जिससे astronomers binary stars तौलते हैं: T और r नापिए, और m one plus m two पढ़िए।
Reduced mass define कीजिए, mu बराबर m one m two over total mass। यह two-body problem को mass mu के एक single body में घटा देता है जो एक fixed centre के चारों ओर orbit करता है।
तो period है two pi root r cubed over big G into total mass, और bound binary की total energy है minus big G m one m two over two r।

<curious>और ख़ूबसूरत limit: जब एक mass दूसरे से बहुत ज़्यादा हो, reduced mass छोटे mass की ओर जाता है, और भारी body fixed centre बन जाता है — बिलकुल वही approximation वापस लाते हुए जो हमने satellites के लिए की।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Worked example: weighing the Earth (CBSE)

board_events.text: Estimate the Earth's mass from surface gravity

board_events.caption: M = gR²/G, from g and R alone
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 450 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="110" cy="100" r="70" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="110" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#22303c">g, R</text>
  <text x="320" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#2b6ca3">M = gR^2 / G</text>
  <text x="320" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#22303c">= (9.8)(6.4×10^6)^2 / (6.67×10^-11)</text>
  <text x="320" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">≈ 6.0×10^24 kg</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A whole planet's mass, from a falling apple and a lab value of G.
This is the celebrated 'weighing of the Earth'.

segments.text: The classic board numerical: estimate the mass of the Earth using the acceleration due to gravity at its surface.
As the figure recalls, the tool is M equals g R squared over big G — nothing but g, R, and the lab value of big G.
We are given g equals nine point eight, R equals six point four times ten to the six metres, and big G equals six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven.
Substitute into M equals g R squared over big G.
The numerator is nine point eight times four point zero nine six times ten to the thirteen, which is four point zero one times ten to the fourteen. Divide by big G.
The mass comes out to about six point zero times ten to the twenty-four kilograms.
Sit with that for a moment: we have deduced a whole planet's mass from a falling apple's acceleration and a laboratory value of big G.
<excited>This is the celebrated weighing of the Earth — a planet weighed without ever leaving its surface.
Classic board numerical: Earth के surface पर acceleration due to gravity का उपयोग करके Earth का mass estimate कीजिए।
जैसा figure याद दिलाता है, tool है M बराबर g R squared over big G — g, R, और big G की lab value के सिवा कुछ नहीं।
हमें दिया है g बराबर nine point eight, R बराबर six point four into ten to the six metres, और big G बराबर six point six seven into ten to the minus eleven।
M बराबर g R squared over big G में substitute कीजिए।
Numerator है nine point eight into four point zero nine six into ten to the thirteen, यानी four point zero one into ten to the fourteen। big G से divide कीजिए।
Mass निकलता है लगभग six point zero into ten to the twenty-four kilograms।
एक पल इसके साथ बैठिए: हमने पूरे planet का mass एक गिरते सेब के acceleration और big G की एक laboratory value से निकाल लिया।
<excited>यही मशहूर weighing of the Earth है — एक planet जो उसकी surface छोड़े बिना तौला गया।

sections.title: Worked example: density from the density form of g (NEET)

board_events.text: Same surface g, twice the radius — what density?

board_events.caption: Use g ∝ Rρ, not g = GM/R²
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 450 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
  <circle cx="95" cy="110" r="34" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.8"/>
  <text x="95" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">Earth</text>
  <text x="95" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">g, R</text>
  <circle cx="270" cy="110" r="66" fill="#e6ebee" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.8"/>
  <text x="270" y="110" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">planet</text>
  <text x="270" y="192" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">same g, R = 2R_E</text>
  <text x="390" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">g ∝ Rρ</text>
  <text x="390" y="128" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b3402f">ρ_p = ρ_E / 2</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A planet has the same surface $g$ as Earth but twice the radius. Find $\rho_p/\rho_E$.
Same $g$ for both, so $R_p\rho_p=R_E\rho_E$.
So the planet's mean density is half the Earth's.
Trap: reaching for $g=GM/R^2$ tangles you in masses — the density form is one line.

segments.text: A NEET ratio problem that rewards picking the right form of g. A planet has the same surface gravity as the Earth but twice the radius. What is the ratio of its mean density to the Earth's?
The figure hints at the shortcut: use the density form of g, not the mass form.
So instead of g equals big G M over R squared, use g equals four thirds pi big G R rho, which means g is proportional to R times rho.
Written as a proportionality, g goes as R rho — the product of radius and density.
Since g is the same for both bodies, the products must be equal: R p rho p equals R E rho E.
Rearrange for the density ratio: rho p over rho E equals R E over R p, which is one half.
So the planet's mean density is half the Earth's — same g, double the radius, half the density.
<whisper>The trap is instinctively reaching for g equals big G M over R squared and getting tangled computing masses. The density form makes it a one-line ratio.
एक NEET ratio problem जो g का सही form चुनने का इनाम देती है। एक planet का surface gravity Earth जैसा है पर radius दोगुना। इसकी mean density का Earth से ratio क्या है?
Figure shortcut का इशारा देता है: g का density form use कीजिए, mass form नहीं।
तो g बराबर big G M over R squared के बजाय, g बराबर four thirds pi big G R rho use कीजिए, जिसका मतलब g, R into rho के proportional है।
एक proportionality के रूप में लिखें, g, R rho के हिसाब से चलता है — radius और density का product।
चूँकि g दोनों bodies के लिए same है, products बराबर होने चाहिए: R p rho p बराबर R E rho E।
Density ratio के लिए rearrange कीजिए: rho p over rho E बराबर R E over R p, यानी one half।
तो planet की mean density Earth की आधी है — same g, दोगुना radius, आधी density।
<whisper>Trap है सहज रूप से g बराबर big G M over R squared की ओर जाना और masses compute करने में उलझ जाना। density form इसे एक-line ratio बना देता है।

board_events.text: Two equal stars, separation d

board_events.caption: Equal masses put the centre of mass at the midpoint
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">

  <text x="220" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">C</text>
  <circle cx="130" cy="120" r="16" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="130" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">M</text>
  <circle cx="310" cy="120" r="16" fill="#c2820a" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="310" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">M</text>
  <line x1="130" y1="145" x2="310" y2="145" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <text x="220" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#22303c">d</text>
  <text x="220" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">equal masses: COM at the midpoint; T = 2π√(d^3/2GM)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Two stars each of mass $M$ orbit their common centre, separation $d$. Find the period.
The total mass is $2M$ — the factor of 2 lives inside the root.
Treating one star as fixed ($T=2\pi\sqrt{d^3/GM}$) is wrong by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.
In a binary, both masses drive the orbit.

segments.text: A JEE Main binary problem that tests the total-mass rule. Two stars, each of mass M, orbit their common centre of mass in a circle, separated by a distance d. Find the period.
As the figure shows, equal masses put the centre of mass exactly at the midpoint, and both stars circle it with the same period.
For a two-body system, the angular velocity satisfies omega squared equals big G times the total mass, over d cubed.
With both masses equal to M, the total mass is two M, so omega squared is two big G M over d cubed.
The period is two pi over omega, which is two pi root d cubed over two big G M.
The crucial detail is that factor of two inside the root — it is the total mass, two M, not a single M.
If you carelessly treat one star as fixed and use two pi root d cubed over big G M, you are wrong by a factor of root two.
<whisper>In a binary, both masses drive the orbit. Always use the sum of the masses in Kepler's third law.
एक JEE Main binary problem जो total-mass rule test करती है। दो stars, हर एक mass M का, अपने common centre of mass के चारों ओर एक circle में orbit करते हैं, distance d से अलग। period निकालिए।
जैसा figure दिखाता है, बराबर masses centre of mass को ठीक midpoint पर रखते हैं, और दोनों stars उसके चारों ओर same period से घूमते हैं।
एक two-body system के लिए, angular velocity satisfy करती है omega squared बराबर big G into total mass, over d cubed।
दोनों masses M के बराबर होने से, total mass two M है, तो omega squared है two big G M over d cubed।
Period है two pi over omega, यानी two pi root d cubed over two big G M।
अहम detail है root के अंदर वो two का factor — यह total mass है, two M, एक single M नहीं।
अगर आप लापरवाही से एक star को fixed मानकर two pi root d cubed over big G M use करते हैं, तो आप root two के factor से ग़लत हैं।
<whisper>एक binary में, दोनों masses orbit चलाते हैं। Kepler के third law में हमेशा masses का sum use कीजिए।

board_events.text: The lighter star traces the bigger circle to keep the balance point fixed.
Negative total energy — bound, as any real binary must be.

segments.text: A full JEE Advanced binary. Two stars of masses m and two m, separated by d, revolve about their common centre of mass. Find each orbital radius, each speed, and the total energy.
The figure sets the geometry. The centre of mass lies closer to the heavier two-m star, so the lighter star swings on the wider circle.
First the radii. From m r one equals two m r two, and r one plus r two equals d, we get r one is two d over three and r two is d over three.
So the lighter star traces the bigger circle — it has to swing wider to keep the balance point fixed.
For the speeds, the common angular velocity is root three big G m over d cubed, and each speed is omega times that star's radius.

Working them out, v one is two thirds root three big G m over d, and v two is one third of the same. So v one equals two v two — the lighter star moves twice as fast, exactly as momentum balance demands.
For the energy, use the compact binary formula: minus big G m one m two over two d, which with masses m and two m gives minus big G m squared over d.
<excited>The total energy is negative, confirming the binary is bound — as any real, stable pair of stars must be.
एक पूरा JEE Advanced binary। masses m और two m के दो stars, d से अलग, अपने common centre of mass के चारों ओर घूमते हैं। हर orbital radius, हर speed, और total energy निकालिए।
Figure geometry set करता है। centre of mass भारी two-m star के क़रीब है, तो हल्का star चौड़े circle पर घूमता है।
पहले radii। m r one बराबर two m r two, और r one plus r two बराबर d से, हमें मिलता है r one है two d over three और r two है d over three।
तो हल्का star बड़ा circle बनाता है — उसे balance point fixed रखने के लिए चौड़ा घूमना पड़ता है।
Speeds के लिए, common angular velocity है root three big G m over d cubed, और हर speed है omega into उस star का radius।
इन्हें निकालने पर, v one है two thirds root three big G m over d, और v two उसी का one third। तो v one बराबर two v two — हल्का star दोगुनी तेज़ चलता है, बिलकुल जैसा momentum balance माँगता है।
Energy के लिए, compact binary formula use कीजिए: minus big G m one m two over two d, जो masses m और two m के साथ देता है minus big G m squared over d।
<excited>Total energy negative है, पुष्टि करते हुए कि binary bound है — जैसा कोई भी असली, stable stars का जोड़ा होना चाहिए।

sections.subtopic: The Gravitational Constant and Two-Body Systems
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for G and two-body systems

board_events.text: Constant and binary: traps and shortcuts
1. Orbits give only $GM$ — $G$ itself needs a lab (Cavendish) experiment.
2. Binary Kepler uses the SUM: $T=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/G(m_1+m_2)}$, not one mass.
3. Heavier star orbits the SMALLER circle: $r\propto 1/m$ — do not swap them.
4. For 'same g' or 'same density', use $g=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi GR\rho$, not $GM/R^2$.
To weigh anything in space, find its orbit: $M=4\pi^2 r^3/GT^2$.
Sun from Earth's orbit, Earth from the Moon, a binary's total from its period.
Reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ turns two bodies back into one.

segments.text: Let us close the chapter's final subtopic with its traps and shortcuts.

Trap one: thinking orbits alone can give big G. Planetary and satellite data only fix the product big G M. The value of big G must come from a lab experiment between known masses — Cavendish. That is why big G was historically the last of the trio to be pinned down.

Trap two: using single-body Kepler for a binary. For two comparable masses, the period uses the total mass, two pi root r cubed over big G times m one plus m two. Forgetting the sum gives a root-two-type error.

Trap three: getting the centre-of-mass radii backwards. The heavier star orbits on the smaller circle, since radius is inversely proportional to mass. Many students assign the bigger orbit to the bigger mass — exactly wrong.

Trap four: confusing the density and inverse-square forms of g. For same-gravity or same-density planet comparisons, four thirds pi big G R rho is far faster than big G M over R squared. Choose the form that isolates what you are comparing.
Now the master shortcut: to weigh anything in space, find its orbit. The central mass is four pi squared r cubed over big G T squared.
The Sun's mass from the Earth's orbit, the Earth's mass from the Moon's orbit, a binary's total mass from its period — all from that one formula.
<whisper>And remember: the reduced mass, m one m two over the total, turns any two-body problem back into a single-body one, so every earlier energy and angular-momentum formula applies unchanged.
chapter के आख़िरी subtopic को उसके traps और shortcuts के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं।

Trap one: यह सोचना कि orbits अकेले big G दे सकती हैं। planetary और satellite data सिर्फ़ product big G M तय करते हैं। big G की value ज्ञात masses के बीच एक lab experiment से आनी चाहिए — Cavendish। इसीलिए big G ऐतिहासिक रूप से तिकड़ी में आख़िरी था जो pin हुआ।

Trap two: एक binary के लिए single-body Kepler use करना। दो comparable masses के लिए, period total mass use करता है, two pi root r cubed over big G into m one plus m two। sum भूलना एक root-two-type error देता है।

Trap three: centre-of-mass radii को उल्टा करना। भारी star छोटे circle पर orbit करता है, क्योंकि radius, mass के inversely proportional है। कई students बड़ी orbit को बड़े mass को देते हैं — बिलकुल ग़लत।

Trap four: g के density और inverse-square forms को confuse करना। same-gravity या same-density planet comparisons के लिए, four thirds pi big G R rho, big G M over R squared से कहीं तेज़ है। वो form चुनिए जो आपकी comparison वाली quantity को अलग करे।
अब master shortcut: space में किसी भी चीज़ को तौलने के लिए, उसकी orbit ढूँढिए। central mass है four pi squared r cubed over big G T squared।
Earth की orbit से Sun का mass, Moon की orbit से Earth का mass, इसके period से एक binary का total — सब उसी एक formula से।
<whisper>और याद रखिए: reduced mass, m one m two over total, किसी भी two-body problem को वापस single-body में बदल देता है, तो हर पहले वाला energy और angular-momentum formula बिना बदले लागू होता है।
